description:
Symptoms and Diagnostic Features:

1. LEAF SYMPTOMS (Early Stage):
   - Initial appearance: Lower leaf surface
   - Appearance: Velvety brown to olive green or mousy black spots
   - Progression: Spots become more definite in outline
   - Color change: Dark brown to black with age
   - Spread: Develops on both leaf surfaces

2. LEAF SYMPTOMS (Advanced Stage):
   - Leaf color: Turns yellowish brown
   - Premature drop: Midsummer defoliation
   - 'Sheet scab': Entire leaf surface covered with velvety black lesions
   - Severe cases: Complete leaf coverage

3. FRUIT SYMPTOMS (Early Spring):
   - Initial location: Calyx end
   - Appearance: Dark olive green spots
   - Shape evolution: Becomes almost circular
   - Color development: Brown to black
   - Texture: Corky surface

4. FRUIT SYMPTOMS (Advanced Stage):
   - Fruit deformation: Becomes disfigured and knotty
   - Surface cracks: Develops in severely infected fruits
   - Marketability: Greatly reduced
   - Storage potential: Poor

5. SHOOT ASSESSMENT (For Monitoring):
   - Autumn assessment: Check for infected leaves on shoots
   - Threshold: >10% shoots with scab indicates high ascospore supply
   - Early June assessment: Scan 100 shoots
   - Diagnostic: 2 shoots with scab spots = 2% infestation

6. SEASONAL PROGRESSION:
   - Spring: Primary infection from ascospores
   - Summer: Secondary spread via conidia
   - Fruit symptoms: Visible from early spring to harvest
   - Leaf symptoms: Progressive through growing season

7. DIFFERENTIAL DIAGNOSIS:
   - Distinguish from: Alternaria leaf spot, Marssonina blotch
   - Key feature: Velvety texture of lesions
   - Characteristic: Olive green to black color progression
   - Pattern: Often starts at calyx end of fruits

You'll notice drying and dropping of flowers and tender fruits. Infected apples turn dull with coarser skin, and when heavily infected show deep cracks and gradually shrivel. Tender nuts become deformed on the shell, and lesions turn grey on infected apples and nuts.
label: DISEASE

description: shows early symptoms of reddish-brown shiny water-soaked lesions and resin exudation on affected parts. Infected shoots appear as 'hanging nuts' which may act as disease sources for the next season. The disease attacks all young and tender vegetative organs including nuts and pseudo fruits/apples.
label: DISEASE

description: symptoms include withering of panicles followed by progressive   of small flower stalks starting from the tips and advancing downward to the main floral shoots. The normal greenish color of healthy shoots progressively turns brown, resulting in flower loss. Infected young nuts and apples become black and fluffy, remaining attached to floral stalks. Heavy infection appears similar to fire damage.
label: DISEASE

description: forms angular to irregular lesions on mature leaves. The lesions are reddish-brown on the upper surface and pale gray to whitish on the underside. Over time, lesions become thinner, papery, and necrotic. They mostly appear on leaf tips and enlarge gradually, expanding downward to cover more than half the leaf. Severe infection may cause defoliation.
label: DISEASE

description: Infected plantlets cease to grow and wither gradually, showing circular water-soaked stripes on the root collar. The roots may rot, leading to lodging (falling over) of the plants. This disease mainly affects young cashew seedlings in nurseries with poor drainage or container-raised young plants.
label: DISEASE

description: Infected cashew leaves develop silver/grey lesions with dark reddish-brown margins that enlarge and coalesce, causing defoliation. Infected young nuts blacken, while older nuts develop characteristic dark lesions. Under favorable conditions, white spore masses of the fungus form within the nut lesions.
label: DISEASE

description: Infected plants show gradual loss of natural green color, with leaves turning yellow (chlorosis) on some branches. From a distance, affected trees appear yellow and green. Within three to four weeks, the entire tree wilts. The disease can spread to nearby trees until all trees in the field are wilted.
label: DISEASE

description: infests all tender tissues of cashew trees, mainly tender leaves and inflorescence including parts not well unfolded. The disease seldom attacks old and mature leaves, preferring young, actively growing tissues.
label: DISEASE

description: attacks all young and tender vegetative organs including shoots, nuts, and pseudo fruits (apples). It does not typically affect mature, hardened tissues, focusing instead on actively growing plant parts.
label: DISEASE

description: Pestalotia lesions mostly appear on the leaf tip and enlarge gradually, coalescing and expanding from the leaf tip downward to cover more than half of the leaf. Masses of conidia appear on both lower and upper sides of the leaves.
label: DISEASE

description: Symptoms: Chlorosis (yellowing) starts at leaf margins and spreads inward. Severe deficiency causes older leaves to turn completely pale yellow and dry. Correction: Apply foliar spray of Potassium Chloride (KCl) at 1% concentration. Ensure balanced soil fertilization based on soil tests to prevent recurrence.
label: NUTRIENT

description: Symptoms: Chlorosis appears first on young leaves, which turn pale yellow to almost white while veins may remain green. Correction: Apply foliar spray of Ferrous Sulphate (FeSO4) at 0.5% concentration.   is common in alkaline soils, so soil pH adjustment may also be necessary.
label: NUTRIENT

description: The mosquito bug (Helopeltis antonii) is the most serious pest of cashew in India, causing more than 30% economic loss through inflorescence blight and immature nut drop. It damages approximately 25% of shoots, 30% of inflorescences, and 15% of tender nuts, making it the single most economically damaging pest.
label: PEST

description: Mosquito bug eggs are reniform (kidney-shaped) and creamy white. The female inserts them deep into tender tissues of new shoots, leaf petioles, and veins. The key identifying feature is the presence of chorionic threads projecting outside the plant tissues, which indicate eggs are embedded within.
label: PEST

description: The mosquito bug completes its lifecycle in 25-32 days under optimal conditions (24-32°C, 50-100% RH). This includes: egg incubation (5-7 days), nymphal period with 5 instars (10-15 days), and adult lifespan (females 7 days, males 9-10 days).
label: PEST

description: Adult mosquito bugs feed primarily during early morning hours (6-10 AM). Each adult makes approximately 150 feeding punctures per day. Both nymphs and adults suck sap from leaves, young shoots, inflorescences, and developing nuts and apples.
label: PEST

description: Symptoms include: 1) Necrotic black lesions at feeding sites (turn pinkish-brown in 24 hours, black in 2-3 days), 2) Gum exudation from feeding punctures, 3) Crinkling of tender leaves, 4) Blackening and death of inflorescences, 5) Shoot die-back, and 6) Immature nut drop. Heavily infested trees appear scorched.
label: PEST

description: The stem and root borer (Plocaederus ferrugineus) is considered the most serious pest because it's an internal tissue borer that can kill trees outright. Its damage results in tree death, and infestation is particularly severe in neglected plantations. Unlike other pests, it directly threatens tree survival rather than just yield.
label: PEST

description: The eggs are whitish, ovoid, and about 3 mm long, resembling rice grains. Females lay 60-90 eggs by inserting them into live tissues in bark crevices at the collar region and exposed roots above soil. Egg period lasts 4-7 days.
label: PEST

description: Grubs feed for 4-7 months inside tree tissues. They bore into bark, feed on sapwood, and create irregular tunnels (deepest in middle, shallow at sides). Mature grubs are off-white, 7-10 cm long, and eventually descend to the root zone to pupate in heartwood chambers.
label: PEST

description: Adults are medium-sized (25-40 mm long) reddish-brown longicorn beetles. Males have antennae twice as long as their body, while female antennae don't surpass body length. They produce a distinctive squeaking sound by rubbing prothorax and mesothorax together. Adults emerge mainly during monsoon (November-June).
label: PEST

description: Symptoms include: 1) Small holes at collar region with frass extrusion, 2) Gummosis (gum oozing from bark), 3) Yellowing and shedding of leaves, 4) Drying of twigs, 5) Gradual tree death. Vascular damage blocks sap flow, leading to decline. Trees over 2 years old are vulnerable, with peak infestation in summer.
label: PEST

description: The leaf miner (Acrocercops syngramma) primarily damages tender foliage of post-monsoon flushes. Nursery seedlings and young plantations are more susceptible than older trees. The pest causes serious damage to young leaves, affecting photosynthesis and plant vigor.
label: PEST

description: Newly hatched larvae are pale white with brownish-yellow heads. At maturity, they turn cherry red, are cylindrical (tapering posteriorly), and 5-9 mm long. Larvae remain active under leaf 'blisters' they create, with a larval period of 10-15 days before dropping to ground for pupation.
label: PEST

description: The leaf miner completes its lifecycle in 20-25 days: larval period (10-15 days), pupal period (7-9 days), plus egg incubation and adult stages. Adults are silver-grey moths that lay eggs on tender leaves.
label: PEST

description: Symptoms include: 1) Tortuous, greyish-white mines on upper leaf surface, 2) Swollen epidermal layers forming blistered patches, 3) Large holes in mature infested leaves, 4) Shriveling, drying, and premature shedding. Typically 3-8 blisters with up to 8 caterpillars per leaf.
label: PEST

description: Mosquito bug nymphs have 5 instars: 1st instar (1.9 days), 2nd (2.2 days), 3rd (2.8 days), 4th (2.8 days), and 5th (3.2 days). Total nymphal period is 13-15 days. Nymphs are wingless, ant-like, orange-colored when young, with about 60% surviving to adulthood.
label: PEST

description: Fully fed grubs descend to root zone, bore into heartwood, and create oval chambers with circular exit holes. Chambers are packed with fibrous tissue and frass, containing a calcarious cocoon where pupation occurs. Pupal period lasts 2-4 months, with adults emerging during monsoon rains (November-June).
label: PEST

description: Most caterpillars drop to the ground and pupate in soil within thin membranous cocoons. Some may pupate in leaf folds. They secrete a protective membranous covering during pupation. The pupal period lasts 7-9 days before adults emerge.
label: PEST

description: 1) Mosquito bug: Active throughout but damaging during vegetative and flowering stages. 2) Stem borer: Peak infestation in summer months, though present year-round. 3) Leaf miner: Most damaging on post-monsoon flushes. Understanding these patterns helps time monitoring and control measures effectively.
label: PEST

description: Whitish or pinkish growth of fungus appears on affected branches. After heavy rains, a film of silky threads can be seen on branches. In advanced stages, bark splits and peels off. Affected branches turn yellow and shed leaves, giving a barren appearance to portions of the tree.
label: DISEASE

description: Disease occurs in nurseries where drainage conditions are poor. The organisms attack the roots or collar region of seedlings or both regions and cause their death.
label: DISEASE

description: When seedlings are infected by Phytophthora palmivora, they become pale. Water-soaked lesions appear at the collar region which turn dark and girdle the stem. Seedlings droop and ultimately die.
label: DISEASE

description: On leaves, water-soaked lesions can be observed in severe cases. These lesions enlarge and coalesce, often covering the entire leaf lamina.
label: DISEASE

description: The fungus infests tender leaves, twigs, and inflorescences. It forms reddish-brown, water-soaked lesions on affected regions. Tender leaves become crinkled and fruits shriveled. Infected inflorescences turn black.
label: DISEASE

description: On the affected region, exudation of resin can be seen. The lesions enlarge and kill the shoots. Repeated infection of terminal shoots can lead to death of the tree over time.
label: DISEASE

description: The characteristic symptom is drying of floral branches. Symptoms appear as minute water-soaked lesions on the main rachis and secondary rachis. The lesions are pinkish-brown, enlarge, and soon turn scabby. Gummy exudates can be seen at affected regions.
label: DISEASE

description: The lesions develop into bigger patches and result in drying up of the inflorescences. The incidence is very severe when cloudy weather prevails.
label: DISEASE

description: During the south-west monsoon months of June-August, extensive leaf fall and shoot rot symptoms are observed.
label: DISEASE

description: Black elongate lesions first develop on the stem with exudation of gum. Later, infection spreads up and down, causing tender stems to collapse and tender leaves to shrivel up.
label: DISEASE

description: Lower mature leaves are infected with black elongated lesions on the midrib, which later spread to the main lateral veins and the leaf blade. The infected leaves are soon shed.
label: DISEASE

description: The leaf and blossom webber (Lamida moncusalis) is reported as a major pest particularly in East-Coast states: Tamil Nadu, Andhra Pradesh, and Odisha. Another species, Orthaga exvinacea, has also been recorded but is of minor importance.
label: PEST

description: Eggs are yellowish-green when freshly laid, ovoid and somewhat flat (0.85 x 0.59 mm). One day later, three broad pink bands appear across the surface. They are laid singly or in groups of 3-5 on the ventral leaf surface or tender shoots, glued finely to the surface. Each female lays 18-83 eggs.
label: PEST

description: The lifecycle is completed in 37-41 days: egg incubation (4-7 days), larval period with 5 instars (16-24 days), pre-pupal period (1-4 days), and pupal period (9-14 days). Adults emerge by rupturing the pupal case.
label: PEST

description: Caterpillars web together new flushes and inflorescences with silken threads, remaining inside to feed. The webbed portions dry up. Silken galleries reinforced with castings and plant scraps indicate caterpillar presence inside. Damage is particularly severe on young trees.
label: PEST

description: Flower thrips (Rhynchothrips raoensis) infestation accounts for 16% fruit drop: 2% in mustard stage, 12% in peanut stage, and 2% in later stages. Their feeding causes scab formation, corky layers, improper kernel filling, nut malformation, and premature fruit drop.
label: PEST

description: Adults and nymphs suck sap from leaves, inflorescences, apples, and nuts. Their rasping-sucking activity causes leaves to turn pale brown, creates scabs on floral branches, apples, and nuts, and forms corky layers. Severe infestations lead to leaf shedding and tree stunting.
label: PEST

description: Foliage thrips (Selenothrips rubrocinctus) eggs are inserted singly into leaf epidermis and covered with a drop of excremental fluid that dries to form a black disc-like pellicle. This protective covering helps identify egg sites on leaves.
label: PEST

description: Nymphs (red-banded thrips) are greenish-yellow with distinctive bright red bands across the first and last abdominal segments. They carry a droplet of excremental fluid at the abdomen tip, deposited periodically to create small brown stains. They feed for about 10 days.
label: PEST

description: Population increases during dry season from December-January, peaks in April-May, and declines rapidly during wet season. They prefer post-monsoon flushes (full-sized but not mature leaves) and avoid old leaves. Young plants suffer heavy damage, especially in summer months.
label: PEST

description: The fruit and nut borer (Thylocoptila paurosema) causes up to 10% yield loss during years of severe infestation in certain regions. It bores into tender apples and nuts, causing shriveling, drying, and premature drop.
label: PEST

description: Young larvae scrape epidermis at nut-apple joints before boring inside. They feed on tender apples and nuts, causing affected nuts to shrivel, dry, and drop prematurely. Entry holes are typically plugged with excreta and located near the apple-nut junction.
label: PEST

description: The major species is Ferrisia virgata (tailed mealybug). Two other species include Planococcus lilacinus and Planococcus citri. They are known by local names like 'chappathi poochi', 'maavupoochi', and 'kallipoochi' in Tamil Nadu.
label: PEST

description: Total lifecycle is 45-65 days: eggs hatch within a day into crawlers, nymphal period lasts 26-45 days, and adults live 15-20 days. Females lay 100-300 eggs in masses covered with cottony white filaments.
label: PEST

description: Mealybugs excrete honeydew (sweet sticky substance) that falls on leaves, twigs, and fruits. This clogs stomata and promotes black sooty mold growth, which reduces photosynthesis. Ants attracted to honeydew spread mealybugs. Terminal leaves turn pale yellow and curl downward from sap loss.
label: PEST

description: Metanastria hyrtaca is the most serious species. Others include Circula trifenestrata, Bombotelia jacosatrix, Lymantria sp., and Thalassodes quadraris. These cause defoliation, often on isolated trees in specific localities.
label: PEST

description: Eggs are spherical, ash-grey to black, with average diameter of 1.83 mm. They adhere closely together with smooth surfaces featuring 3 deep brown circular spots arranged triangularly. Eggs hatch in 9 days.

description: Caterpillars are nocturnal, gregarious feeders that congregate on leaf undersides. Initially they feed halfway through leaves leaving midribs intact; later they voraciously consume entire leaves and tender twigs, causing complete defoliation. Dark green, pea-sized fecal pellets littered under trees indicate infestation.
label: PEST

description: Total lifecycle averages 66 days (range 55-75 days): egg (9 days), larval (40-45 days), pre-pupal (2-3 days), pupal (12-18 days), and adult (2-7 days). Females lay 180-300 eggs within 48 hours after mating.

description: The leaf folder (Sylepta aurantiacalis) is active from September to January, synchronizing with flushing and flowering seasons. It's a major pest among six leaf folder species attacking cashew.
label: PEST

description: Caterpillars roll tender leaves from tip downward or longitudinally, fastening them with silken threads to form tubular niches. One caterpillar inhabits each roll, feeding on green tissues by scraping. The fed matter visible through their transparent integument makes them appear green.

description: Look for withering of the spindle with pale color, brown and bent spear leaf, foul smell from the affected area, rotting of the bud, and eventually the palm may die. The disease is caused by Phytophthora palmivora and spreads through rain splash.

description: Look for yellowing and wilting of older leaves, internal stem discoloration when you cut the trunk, reddish-brown ooze or bleeding from the stem, and trunk rot. This is caused by Ganoderma and Thielaviopsis fungi that enter through wounds.

description: Caterpillars cause leaf drying, create silken galleries on leaves, severe defoliation, and scraping damage to leaf tissue. Species like Opisina arenosella, Contheyla rotunda, and others feed extensively, especially during monsoon.

description: Major species include Opisina arenosella, Contheyla rotunda, Parasa lepida, and Macroplectra nararia. Some have stinging hairs. All feed on leaf tissue creating silken galleries and causing defoliation.

description: Dig and examine roots for lesions, rotting, and browning. General decline, yellowing leaves, and button shedding above ground indicate nematode damage below. Send soil and root samples to lab for Radopholus similis detection.

label: PEST

description: Parasa lepida larvae are greenish with white lines and four rows of spiny scoli tipped red/black. Adults have green wings with dark basal patches. Contheyla rotunda larvae are black/grey dorsally; adults are greyish-brown with dark forewings having black points.

description: Gangara thyrsis larvae are pale green with reddish markings and white waxy covering; adults are chocolate brown with yellow spots. Suastus gremius larvae are smooth green with head-body constriction; adults are chocolate brown with yellow forewing spots.

description: Adults are brown colored beetles with striated wings that do not fully cover the abdomen. They are attracted to trees like neem, Ailanthus, and Acacia during monsoon showers.

description: Adults are cream-colored, tiny insects resembling ants with dark colored heads. They are often seen swarming during specific seasons, particularly after rains.

description: Nymphs are white with dark patches. Adults are white-colored insects with distinctive netted venation on their wings, giving them a lace-like appearance.

description: Nymphs are covered with circular waxy secretions that form protective scales. These scales can be scraped off to reveal the soft-bodied insect underneath.

description: **Symptoms:** Uniform light green to yellowing (chlorosis) starting from the tips of the oldest lower leaves, progressing upwards. label: DISEASE

description: specifically affects only matured or old leaves of mango trees. The disease does not appear on young leaves, making it distinct from other foliar diseases. The fungus shows preference for older foliage, where it causes spot formation with characteristic dark margins and dull grey necrotic centers.
label: DISEASE

description: disease in mango is caused by the fungus Fusarium subglutinans. This pathogen causes two types of  : vegetative   affecting young seedlings with abnormal swollen growth and short internodes, and floral   where flower buds transform into vegetative buds creating a witches' broom appearance with dull green buds that seldom open.
label: DISEASE

description: Vegetative   is most pronounced in young seedlings. At this stage, affected plants develop abnormal vegetative growth that is swollen with very short internodes, creating a bunched, compact appearance. Seedlings are particularly vulnerable to this form of   caused by Fusarium subglutinans, which can affect their overall development and vigor.
label: DISEASE

description: on stored fruits appears as black spots that are initially round but later coalesce to form large irregular blotches, sometimes covering the entire fruit surface. The spots have large deep cracks where the fungus penetrates deep into the fruit, causing extensive rotting. Under moist conditions, the blackened areas become covered with minute pinkish reproductive bodies of the fungus. You may also observe staining, russetting, and tear streaking involving only the skin of the fruit.
label: DISEASE

description: caused by Diplodia natalensis starts at the base of the pedicel (stem attachment point). A circular brown area develops near the stem end, which gradually expands as a dark brown to black area towards the lower portion of the fruit and may eventually cover the entire fruit surface. The rotting is very fast - the entire fruit can rot within 2-3 days. The disease is observed only on ripe fruits. It may also start from points other than the stem end if the fruit gets bruised.
label: DISEASE

description: caused by Aspergillus niger shows characteristic yellowing with irregular dull grayish spots that develop into black necrotic areas with growth of black mould. The tissue below and around the spots disintegrates and emits a foul odor. The fruits rot very fast. Rotting may start from any point but injury is essential for the disease to begin. It may also start from the stem end as a natural opening exists there.
label: DISEASE

description: typically starts at the base of the pedicel (stem end) where a circular brown area develops and spreads. However, the disease may also start from points other than the stem end when fruits get bruises or injuries. The stem end is the primary infection site because it provides a natural opening for the pathogen Diplodia natalensis to enter, especially when fruits are harvested without proper stalk retention.
label: DISEASE

description: Under moist conditions,   symptoms become more pronounced with the blackened areas becoming covered with minute pinkish reproductive bodies of the fungus. Moisture favors fungal growth and sporulation. The pathogen creates deep cracks in the spots where it penetrates deep into the fruit, causing extensive rotting. High humidity during storage accelerates disease development from latent infections.
label: DISEASE

description: is distinguished by: (1) Characteristic yellowing with irregular dull grayish spots that develop into black necrotic areas, (2) Growth of distinctive black mould (Aspergillus niger), (3) Tissue disintegration below and around spots that emits a foul odor - this smell is a key diagnostic feature, (4) Requirement of injury for infection to start, and (5) Very fast rotting once established. The combination of black mould growth and foul odor is particularly characteristic of Aspergillus rot.
label: DISEASE

description: caused by Diplodia natalensis is observed only on ripe fruits. The disease does not affect immature or green fruits. This specificity for ripe fruits is important for timing control measures and understanding disease risk - fruits become susceptible as they ripen, making postharvest management and proper storage conditions critical during the ripening period.
label: DISEASE

description: causes several types of skin symptoms on mango fruits: (1) Staining - discoloration of the fruit skin, (2) Russetting - rough, brownish patches on the skin surface, and (3) Tear streaking - streak-like patterns on the skin. These symptoms involve only the skin of the fruit and are attributed to Colletotrichum gloeosporioides. These surface symptoms may appear alongside or separate from the deeper rotting symptoms with black spots and cracks.
label: DISEASE

description: symptoms become visible when mango fruits attain some size. A small etiolated (pale) area develops near the distal end (tip) of the fruit, which gradually spreads and turns nearly black, covering the tip of the fruit completely. The black area remains hard and the growth of the fruit is checked. This disorder is also known as chimney disease and is particularly visible on cultivars like Dushehri.
label: DISEASE

description: caused by boron deficiency shows: (1) First, water-soaked grayish spots develop on the lower side of the fruit, (2) Later, spots enlarge and develop into dark brown necrotic areas, (3) Internal tissue starts disintegrating, (4) The pericarp and mesocarp disintegrate, exposing the flesh, (5) Yellow colored droplets come out, and (6) Affected fruits drop easily from the tree.
label: DISEASE

description: (Jhumka) is characterized by formation of several fruitlets at the tip of the panicle. The fruitlets are darker green in color and their shape is slightly curved compared to normal fruits. These fruits generally hang for more time compared to normal fruits but do not grow further and eventually drop. The fruits do not have seed formation. This disorder is particularly visible in Dushehari cultivar.
label: DISEASE

description: s are characterized by woody growths of 10-15 inches diameter formed on limbs and branches. The cause is not known. Galls are abundant on cultivars like Chinnasuvarnarekha and Langra, and moderate in Neelam. These large galls can cause branches to break near the gall sites, potentially damaging the tree structure.
label: DISEASE

description: (also called soft nose) is severe in late maturing varieties like Neelam and Mallika, particularly in delayed harvest, leading to substantial loss. Numerous red-nosed fruits are seen on trees during the end of summer with onset of showers. The   gradually becomes soft and rots. Fruits with   are unfit for export. The cause is not known.
label: DISEASE

description: are growths of pea to marble size that develop on the fruit and are very unsightly. The stylar end (bottom) part of the fruit is much affected while the stem end is practically free from tumors. The cause of this disorder is not known. These tumors reduce the market value and aesthetic quality of the fruit.
label: DISEASE

description: (softening of tissue) is characterized by the pulp near the stone becoming jelly-like with tissue disintegration while the outer pulp near the peel remains normal. The taste becomes repulsive and fruits lose table quality. From the outer appearance, fruits look normal - the disorder is internal. Dashehari cultivar is more susceptible compared to others like Chausa and Langra. Incidence is higher in Lucknow region, particularly in late harvested fruits.
label: DISEASE

description: , also called internal breakdown, is a serious malady affecting Alphonso mango, which is the main export cultivar. It occurs in ripe fruits and renders them unfit for consumption. This disorder has become a bottleneck in export and expansion of Alphonso cultivation in Maharashtra and Gujarat where it is grown commercially. Convecting heat arising from soil and intense solar radiation are reported to be the main causes.
label: DISEASE

description: is characterized by scorching of leaf margins, which is the characteristic symptom. Scorching starts from the tip and progresses downwards. Fruit quality is reduced in potassium-deficient trees. Additionally, trees with   are easily prone to pest and disease attack due to weakened plant health.
label: NUTRIENT

description: symptoms include: (1) Leaves become small and narrow with margins bent upward or downward, (2) Internodal length is reduced drastically, (3) Twigs with crowded leaves give a rosette appearance, (4) Pale interveinal areas and green veins are typical, (5) Trees with zinc hunger do not grow well, and (6) Yield, size, and quality of fruits are reduced. Small plants with severe   may die. This deficiency is conspicuously seen in alkaline, saline, and sandy soils.
label: NUTRIENT

description: Fruits affected by   (boron deficiency) drop easily because: (1) The internal tissue disintegrates, weakening fruit structure, (2) The pericarp and mesocarp breakdown, compromising fruit integrity, (3) Yellow colored droplets exude from the fruit, indicating severe tissue degradation, and (4) The water-soaked spots that develop into dark brown necrotic areas weaken the attachment to the tree. This tissue breakdown causes premature fruit drop.
label: DISEASE

description: Clustered fruits (Jhumka) differ from normal fruits in several ways: (1) Multiple fruitlets form at the tip of the panicle instead of single fruits, (2) They are darker green in color, (3) Their shape is slightly curved compared to normal fruits, (4) They hang for more time on the tree, (5) They do not grow beyond initial size, and (6) They lack seed formation. Eventually, these abnormal fruits drop from the tree.
label: DISEASE

description: s show varying susceptibility among cultivars: (1) Chinnasuvarnarekha - galls are abundant, (2) Langra - galls are abundant, and (3) Neelam - galls are moderate. The severity of gall formation varies by cultivar, with some varieties being more prone to developing these large woody growths on limbs and branches.
label: DISEASE

description: Dashehari cultivar is most susceptible to   (softening of tissue) disorder compared to other cultivars like Chausa and Langra. The problem is particularly severe in the Lucknow region, especially in late harvested fruits. The disorder has been recorded in several mango varieties, but Dashehari shows the highest susceptibility.
label: DISEASE

description: No,   disorder cannot be detected from the outer appearance - affected fruits look completely normal externally. The disorder is internal, with only the pulp near the stone becoming jelly-like with tissue disintegration, while the outer pulp near the peel remains normal. This makes detection difficult without cutting the fruit open, which affects marketability.
label: DISEASE

description: The rosette appearance in   occurs because internodal length is reduced drastically, causing leaves to crowd together on twigs. This creates a bunched or rosette-like pattern where multiple small, narrow leaves cluster at the shoot tip with very short distances between them. Combined with pale interveinal areas and green veins, this distinctive rosette pattern is diagnostic of  .
label: DISEASE

description: In  , leaf margins are bent either upward or downward. This curling or bending of margins, combined with the leaves becoming small and narrow, is a characteristic symptom. The leaves also show pale interveinal areas with green veins remaining, creating a distinctive pattern. These multiple leaf symptoms together help diagnose  .
label: DISEASE

description: In   disorder, the black area that develops at the tip of the fruit remains hard. Unlike soft rots or other fruit disorders where affected tissue becomes soft, the blackened tip maintains a hard texture. Additionally, the growth of the fruit is checked or stopped once   develops, preventing normal fruit development and size increase.
label: DISEASE

description: progresses in stages: (1) First, water-soaked grayish spots develop on the lower side of the fruit, (2) Later, these spots enlarge and develop into dark brown necrotic areas, (3) Internal tissue starts disintegrating, (4) The pericarp and mesocarp disintegrate, exposing the flesh, (5) Yellow colored droplets exude from the fruit, and (6) Finally, affected fruits drop easily. This progressive deterioration is due to boron deficiency.
label: DISEASE

description: severely affects quality and marketability because: (1) The taste becomes repulsive, making fruits unpalatable, (2) Fruits lose table quality completely, (3) The pulp near the stone disintegrates into jelly-like consistency, (4) Despite normal external appearance, the internal defect makes fruits unmarketable, and (5) Detection requires cutting fruit open, which affects sales since consumers cannot identify affected fruits before purchase. This hidden defect causes significant economic loss.
label: DISEASE

description: is a fungus growing on honeydew secreted by sap-sucking pests like leafhoppers, mealybugs, and scale insects. Confirm by inspecting the plant for the underlying pests: look for leafhoppers on flowers, white cottony mealybug masses, or scale insects on leaves/fruits. The black coating itself is a secondary symptom.
label: PEST

description: The Mango Hopper (Idioscopus spp.) is the primary cause. These pests suck sap from flowers and tender shoots, secreting honeydew. The honeydew promotes the growth of black   fungus, and the feeding damage directly causes flower withering and drop.
label: PEST

description: appears as black spots on fruits, flowers, and leaves. These lesions often start as small, dark spots that can enlarge and coalesce, causing blossom blight, leaf spotting, and fruit rot, especially under warm, humid conditions.
label: DISEASE

description: appears as a distinctive white, powdery or flour-like fungal growth on the inflorescence (flower panicles) and young, tender fruits. It can cause flowers to wither and prevent fruit set, or blemish and distort young fruits.
label: DISEASE

description: appears as dark, sunken lesions on leaves, flowers, and fruits. Infected fruits often rot before ripening. The disease is devastating in humid regions, spreading rapidly during warm, moist conditions, especially in the rainy season.
label: DISEASE

description: looks like white powder on leaves, flowers, and fruit. Severe infections cause premature flower and fruit drop. Young leaves may become distorted. It thrives in dry conditions with high humidity during early morning and evening.
label: DISEASE

description: is a secondary fungal infection that grows on honeydew secreted by sap-sucking pests like aphids, mealybugs, and scale insects. The black, sooty layer on leaves blocks sunlight, reducing photosynthesis and weakening the tree, though it doesn't directly infect plant tissue.
label: DISEASE

description: Mango mealybugs (Drosicha mangiferae) suck sap and secrete honeydew. This sugary substance encourages the growth of   fungus, which forms a black layer on leaves that blocks sunlight and reduces photosynthesis.
label: PEST

description: Look for wedge-shaped nymphs and adults on tender shoots and inflorescences. They suck sap, causing reduced plant vigour, flower destruction, and fruit drop. Heavy infestation leads to curling and drying of tissue. A key sign is the excretion of honeydew, which promotes the growth of Sooty Mould on leaves and fruits.
label: PEST

description: Adults and nymphs, covered in whitish powder, colonize tree bark, young shoots, and panicles. They suck sap, causing flower drop and reduced fruit set. Like hoppers, they excrete honeydew, leading to Sooty Mould development on leaves and fruits.
label: PEST

description: Larvae tunnel into and destroy the inflorescence axis, causing it to bend and dry out completely. Later attacks target young fruits (causing yellowing and drop) and tender new leaves. The most severe symptom is the stunting and bending of the entire inflorescence, leading to its destruction.
label: PEST

condition: fruit flies (bactrocera dorsalis, b. correctus, b. zonatus)
description: Female flies puncture the skin of mature fruits to lay eggs. The maggots (larvae) feed on the pulp, causing internal rotting. Infested fruits may develop soft spots, ooze, and drop prematurely. Secondary infections often follow, accelerating decay. Managing this pest also helps reduce Anthracnose disease.
label: PEST

description: Look for clusters of leaves webbed together by silk. Inside these webs, caterpillars feed gregariously, initially scraping the leaf surface and later consuming the entire leaf. Several caterpillars can be found within a single webbed cluster, severely defoliating the shoot.
label: PEST

description: Nymphs suck sap from buds, causing them to develop into hard, conical, green galls. These galls are prominent from September to October and prevent flowering and fruit setting on affected shoots. The nymphs overwinter inside these protective galls.
label: PEST

description: The damage is caused by grubs that feed on bark and make irregular cavities. They create tunnels that may bore upward into stems or branches, resulting in drying and death of affected branches. Initial feeding occurs on the bark before the grubs enter deeper into the wood.
label: PEST

description: Larvae initially bore into young tender leaves and mid-ribs, then tunnel into tender shoots near the growing point. This causes excreta accumulation, leaf dropping, and wilting of terminal shoots. Damage typically occurs from August onward.
label: PEST

description: Look for brown zig-zag ribbon-like silken webs on tree bark composed of excreta and wood particles. Larvae create shelter tunnels inside the bark where they rest and feed.
label: PEST

description: Nymphs and adults suck sap from leaves and tender parts, reducing plant vigor. They excrete honeydew which promotes sooty mould development on leaves and tender parts.
label: PEST

description: Adult weevils are stout, dark brown (5-8 mm). Grubs bore through pulp, feed on seed coat and cotyledons. When cut open, pulp adjacent to affected stone appears discolored. Pupation occurs inside the seed.
label: PEST

condition: thrips (coliothrips indicus, rhipiphorothris cruentatus, scirtothrips dorsalis)
description: Nymphs and adults lacerate tissues and suck cell sap. Leaf-feeding species cause silvery sheen on leaves with small fecal matter spots. S. dorsalis attacks inflorescence and young fruits. Damage appears as feeding marks on mesophyll near leaf tips.
label: PEST

description: Adults are reddish-brown with black head, red thorax, and black/white abdomen. They and nymphs feed on petioles, tender shoots and leaf veins causing necrotic lesions. Eggs are inserted into epidermis of tender shoots and inflorescence axis.
label: PEST

description: Caterpillars (25 mm) have red and white alternating bands. They bore into fruits at the bottom (beak region), feed inside reaching kernels. Entrance hole is plugged with excreta. Affected fruits rot and fall prematurely. Active January-May.
label: PEST

description: Tiny caterpillars mine under the dorsal epidermis of tender leaves, feeding within. This causes grayish-white blister-like appearances on leaves as they feed between leaf layers.
label: PEST

description: Red tree ants web and stitch together several leaves, usually at the top of branches, to build their nests. They are carnivorous and prey on small insects. Indirect damage occurs as they protect honeydew-producing insects like aphids and scales, which can lead to sooty mould development.
label: PEST

condition: inflorescence caterpillars (eucrostus sp., argyroploce aprobola, euproctis fraterna)
description: Caterpillars from multiple species (Geometridae, Eucosmidae, Lymantriidae families) attack and feed on inflorescences. If not controlled, they cause heavy losses through reduced fruit bearing capacity by damaging flowers and young fruitlets.
label: PEST

description: Termites are white, light-shy insects that remain underground or in tunnels. They feed on roots or move upward creating tunnels. They construct characteristic mud galleries on tree trunks, under which they feed on bark. Severe infestations can girdle and kill trees.
label: PEST

description: White superficial powdery fungal growth appears on inflorescence, leaves, stalks and young fruits, causing shedding. Affected flowers fail to open and fall prematurely. Young fruits may be entirely covered; as they grow, epidermis cracks forming corky tissue. Fruits may drop at marble size.
label: DISEASE

description: Young leaves show infection when color changes from brown to light green. White patches appear on both sides, more conspicuous on lower surface. Patches coalesce into larger purple-brown areas, often restricted to veins. Leaves may twist, curl and distort.
label: DISEASE

description: Oval or irregular vinaceous brown to deep brown spots of various sizes scattered over leaf surface. Later lesions become blighted, rupture and show 'shot hole' symptoms. Young leaves are more susceptible than older ones.
label: DISEASE

description: Produces elongated black necrotic areas on twigs. Causes wither tip where young branch tips start drying from tip downwards. Petioles turn grey or black when affected.
label: DISEASE

description: Small black spots appear on panicles and open flowers, gradually enlarging and coalescing to cause blossom blight. Infected flowers fall off, leaving persistent spikes on peduncles.
label: DISEASE

description: Fruit infection is more common during transit and storage. Symptoms appear as dark lesions that can expand during post-harvest handling and storage conditions.
label: DISEASE

description: Profuse oozing of gum on affected wood, bark of trunk and larger branches, especially on cracked areas. In severe cases, gum droplets trickle down stems, bark turns dark brown with longitudinal cracks, rots completely, and trees dry up due to cracking, rotting and girdling effects.
label: DISEASE

description: Circular, slightly angular, elongated spots 2-4mm diameter, brown in color. During rainy season, lesions vary in size, shape and color. On young fruits, infection appears grey to grayish brown with dark irregular margins. As fruits grow, spots enlarge with cracked, fissured, corky centers.
label: DISEASE

description: Black velvety raised fungal outgrowth appears on midribs/veins of leaves, twigs and branches as spots that gradually increase and encircle trunk, limbs, branches and twigs. Creates characteristic black banded appearance. Incidence is low on main branches.
label: DISEASE

description: Leaves become lusterless and sparse. Trees wilt and die gradually. Infected roots are very light, crumble easily and powder with fingers. Fungal brackets (fruiting bodies) appear at tree base during rainy season.
label: DISEASE

description: Sudden dropping of leaves after seedling emergence. During prolonged rainy/humid weather, circular to irregular water-soaked patches appear at/below ground level. Patches enlarge and girdle entire seedling base.
label: DISEASE

description: Rusty red fructification of alga appears on leaves, veins, petioles, young twigs and fruits. Initially spots are greenish-grey and velvety, turning reddish-brown. Algal growth is superficial but conspicuous.
label: DISEASE

description: Found on trunks, branches and twigs of full-grown trees in high humidity, heavy rainfall areas and poorly managed orchards. Appear as whitish, pinkish superficial patches of different shapes.
label: DISEASE

description: Presence of fungal brackets (fruiting bodies) at tree base during rainy season, combined with light, crumbly roots and overall tree decline.
label: DISEASE

description: Leaves lose green color and turn white, a condition called 'bleaching.' Leaf size is reduced. In severe cases, leaves dry from tip downwards. This deficiency is common in high-calcium soils and known as 'calcium induced iron chlorosis.'
label: NUTRIENT

description: Cracking of fruit is the characteristic symptom. Additional symptoms include lusterless leathery leaves with thickened veins and brown areas visible in yellow fruit pulp.
label: NUTRIENT

description: Weak terminal shoots followed by defoliation and die-back of branches on top of long drooping branches. Often occurs with heavy nitrogen fertilization and may accompany Zinc deficiency symptoms.
label: NUTRIENT

description: Females lay up to 200 eggs singly into tissues of young leaves, shoots, flower stalks, and unopened buds. Egg period is 4-7 days. Nymphs are greenish with black or brown markings, cannot fly, and move rapidly on plants. Nymphal period is 8-13 days. Three species exist: A. atkinsoni (4.2-5mm, dark grey, two spots on abdomen), I. clypealis (3.5mm, smallest, two scutellum spots), and I. niveosparsus (4-4.8mm, three scutellum spots, band across wings). Hoppers complete 3-4 generations per season with population buildup in February-April and June-August.
label: PEST

description: Adults and nymphs suck sap from tender shoots and flowers, causing drying and dropping of flowers. They secrete honeydew that develops sooty mould, reducing photosynthesis. Heavy puncturing and continuous sap drainage cause curling and drying of infested tissue. During off-season, hoppers shelter in bark cracks, crevices, or leaf undersides. The damage significantly impacts flowering and fruit set.
label: PEST

description: Females lay up to 150 oval, shining pink eggs in fluted ovisacs attached to their body or in soil. Egg hatching starts at end of December and continues up to a month. First instar nymphs (crawlers) are mobile, climb trees, and immediately start sucking sap forming colonies. Three female and five male nymphal instars exist. Females are hermaphrodites that self-inseminate. Adult longevity is 7 days for males, 15-35 days for females. Females lay eggs for 22-47 days during April-May, then crawl down trees and enter soil cracks.
label: PEST

description: Adult females are oval, flat, body covered with white mealy powder. Adult males have one pair of black wings and are crimson red. Males mate with females. The white powdery appearance on shoots and fruits is characteristic. Nymphs and adults suck plant sap and secrete honeydew that develops sooty mould on infested shoots and fruits.
label: PEST

description: Females lay 15-25 reddish, oval eggs in clusters under loose bark. Eggs hatch in 8-10 days. Larvae are pinkish white with brown spots. Larval period is 9-11 months. Pupae are brown, pupating inside the stem for 3-4 months. Adult males are reddish brown with numerous dark bands on forewings; females are yellowish orange with similar markings.
label: PEST

description: Caterpillars bore into trunk or branch junctions making zigzag galleries. Presence of galleries made of silk and frass is the key symptom. They hide in tunnels during day, emerge at night to feed on bark. Infestation hinders sap flow, arrests plant growth, and drastically reduces fruit formation. Heavy infestations retard tree growth and severely affect fruit yield.
label: PEST

description: Females lay up to 3000 eggs under fruit skin in clusters of 10-50 below surface. Eggs are white, elongate, elliptical, hatching in 1-2 days. Maggots are white, legless, resembling elongated cones. Maggot stage lasts 11-15 days. Pupation occurs in soil. Puparium is yellowish-brown and seed-like with pupal period of about 10 days. Adult prothorax has two lateral vitae. B. dorsalis and B. zonata have two black spots on face; B. correcta has black transverse line. B. dorsalis and B. correcta are dark; B. zonata is orange.
label: PEST

description: Females puncture fruits with pointed ovipositor and insert eggs inside. Infested fruits exhibit puncture marks and oozing. After hatching, maggots feed on fruit pulp, resulting in fruit dropping and rotting. The damage makes fruits unmarketable and can cause significant economic loss if not controlled properly.
label: PEST

description: Females lay 150 eggs singly on vegetative buds, inflorescence buds, inflorescence axis, or in open flowers. Eggs hatch within 2-3 days. Minute maggots penetrate tender parts where eggs were laid and start feeding. Mature larvae drop into soil for pupation. Larval period is 7-10 days; pupal period is 5-7 days. Pupae are yellowish-brown, 1-2mm long, with male pupae smaller than females. Adults are small midges with wing length 1.0-1.5mm. Females have protractible ovipositor.
label: PEST

description: It attacks floral buds, tender fruits, and tender leaves. Infested mango buds, shoots, and young fruits develop many small blister galls, about 3-4mm long, each containing a yellow maggot. In severe attacks, affected plant parts shrivel and die. Small emergence holes may be detected on galls. The damage significantly reduces flowering success and early fruit development.
label: PEST

description: Females lay 250 eggs singly on bark or in cracks and crevices on trunk or branches. Egg period lasts 1-2 weeks. Grubs are yellow, apodous (legless) with 6-month larval period. Pupal period lasts 19-36 days. Adult beetle is greyish with two pink dots and lateral spine on thorax and long antennae reaching body end. Adult longevity is 6 months.
label: PEST

description: Grubs start feeding below bark of branches making tunnels, then bore into main stem. Frass coming out of entry point indicates trunk borer presence. Damage results in yellowing leaves followed by drying of terminal shoots and branches, leading to death of whole tree. Internal tunneling weakens structural integrity of affected parts.
label: PEST

description: Females lay up to 300 eggs singly in small cavities made in young fruit skin and under rind of ripening fruits. Eggs are oval, about 0.8×0.3mm, creamy-white when freshly laid. Grubs are white with curved body, brown heads, and legless. Newly hatched larvae are 1mm long; mature larvae are 17mm long. After hatching, larvae burrow through fruit flesh into seed where they feed until pupation. Grub period is 22-70 days. Pupa is whitish when new, changing to pale red before adult emergence. Pupation occurs in seed within fruit stone. Pupal period is about 7 days. Adult weevils have compact body, dark brown with mottled wing markings, about 8mm long, active at dusk, can fly. Females start laying 3-4 days after mating. Adult longevity is about 60 days. Adults diapause under loose bark on trunks, in branch crevices during non-fruiting season.
label: PEST

description: Larvae are pale green with brown head and prothoracic shield. Adults are brownish moths with wavy lines on forewings. Initially caterpillars feed on leaf surface gregariously by scraping. Later they make webs on tender shoots and leaves together and feed within. Several caterpillars may be found in a single webbed cluster of leaves. This reduces photosynthetic capacity and affects new growth.
label: PEST

description: Eggs are round and cream colored, laid in clusters of 2-6 eggs on fruit. Fecundity ranges from 4-38 eggs. Mature larvae have 11 bands along back, pink at first then turning red. Larval period is about 16 days. Pupation takes place in soil or in/under bark protected with silk cocoon. Pupal period is about 14 days. Brown adult moth is approximately 12mm in size with prominent snout.
label: PEST

description: After hatching, larvae bore into fruits. Caterpillars bore into fruit at bottom (beak region) and feed inside reaching kernels. Entrance hole is plugged with excreta. Affected fruits rot and fall prematurely. This causes significant economic loss due to fruit drop and quality degradation.
label: PEST

description: Females lay up to 180 eggs, about 0.6×0.3mm long, roughly oval, white to pale yellow. Egg period is 4-65 days. Larval body is white to creamy-white, 7.5-10mm long, moderately curved. Pupae are up to 10mm length, varying from white to pale red. Adults are 6-9mm long, mottled brown with long snout. The weevil produces 1 generation per year, completing egg to adult life cycle in 35-53 days.
label: PEST

description: Hatched larvae tunnel through flesh forming a chamber next to seed. From there each larva continues tunneling through mango flesh leaving brown granular feces behind. This internal damage reduces fruit quality and marketability even if external appearance seems normal initially.
label: PEST

description: Nymphs and adult scales suck sap from leaves and other tender parts, reducing plant vigor. They secrete honeydew which helps development of sooty mould. In severe scale infestation, growth and fruit bearing capacity of mango tree is adversely affected. The combined effect of sap removal and sooty mould significantly impacts tree health.
label: PEST

description: is a monophagous pest of mango in northern India. Nymphs emerge during August-September and suck cell sap from adjacent buds. As a result of feeding, buds develop into hard conical green galls usually seen during September-October. Consequently, there is no flowering and fruit setting. Nymphs overwinter inside galls.
label: PEST

description: Nymphs and adults lacerate tissues and suck oozing cell sap. Thrips feed on leaves, inflorescence, and young fruits. Leaf-feeding species feed on mesophyll tissues near leaf tips. Affected leaves show silvery shine, leaf edges curl upward, and bear small spots of fecal matter. Affected fruits show corky appearance, reducing marketability.
label: PEST

description: s (Oecophylla smaragdina) web and stitch together a few leaves at branch tops to build nests. Ants are carnivorous and prey upon small insects, which is beneficial. However, indirect damage is caused by protecting insects like aphids and scales which excrete honeydew. The ants farm these honeydew-producing insects, increasing their populations.
label: PEST

description: It attacks leaves, flowers, panicle stalks, and fruits, causing superficial white powdery appearance. Disease spreads rapidly by wind. Infection typically starts from inflorescence and spreads downward covering floral axis, tender leaves, and soft stem. Flowers fail to open, blacken or become brown, dry, and may fall from panicles. This significantly reduces fruit set.
label: DISEASE

description: Disease occurs when rains or mists are accompanied by cooler nights during flowering, especially when weather is cool and dry. Minimum temperature of 13-15°C, maximum temperature of 23-25°C with moderate relative humidity (64-72%) favors disease development. Pathogen survives in affected plant debris and under favorable conditions, airborne conidia are disseminated by wind.
label: DISEASE

description: On leaves: lesions start as small, angular, brown to black spots that enlarge to form extensive dead areas. On panicles: first symptoms are small black or dark-brown spots which enlarge, coalesce, and kill flowers before fruit production. Petioles, twigs, and stems are susceptible and develop typical black color. Twig dieback occurs when severe, elongated, blackened lesions form on stems and twigs die back apically. On ripe fruits: sunken, prominent, dark brown to black decay spots develop; fruits may drop prematurely.
label: DISEASE

description: Under favorable climatic conditions of high humidity, frequent rains, and temperature of 24-32°C coinciding with flowering,   infections occur in the field. The pathogen survives between seasons on infected and defoliated branch terminals and mature leaves. These serve as inoculum sources for new infections.
label: DISEASE

description: Two types exist: 1) Vegetative Malformation: more common on young seedlings, characterized by disrupting apical growth resulting in several small flushes. Multi-branching of shoot apex with scaly leaves is known as 'Bunchy Top' or 'Witches' Broom'. Malformed seedlings remain stunted and die. 2) Floral Malformation: shows variation in panicle. Malformed head dries up in black mass and persists for long time.
label: DISEASE

description: Disease spreads through propagating materials. The fungus doesn't sporulate in situ but sporulates on dried malformed panicles. Disease is severe at temperatures between 10-15°C during December to January before flowering. Disease is mild in areas with 15-20°C, sporadic between 20-25°C. Plants at 4-8 years are susceptible. In some cases, mites have been reported to carry the fungus and cause spread.
label: DISEASE

description: Disease is noticed on leaves, leaf stalks, stems, twigs, branches, and fruits, initially producing water-soaked lesions, later turning into typical canker. Water-soaked irregular to angular raised lesions measuring 1-4mm in diameter form. Lesions are light yellow initially with yellow halo but with age enlarge or coalesce to form irregular necrotic cankerous patches with dark brown color. Water-soaked, dark brown to black lesions are observed which gradually develop into cankerous, raised or flat spots. These spots often burst, extruding gummy substances containing highly contagious bacterial cells.
label: DISEASE

description: Bacteria enters through natural openings such as stomata, wax and oil glands, leaf and fruit abrasions, leaf scars, and at apex of branches in panicle. Periods of high humidity, surface wetness, and wind accompanied with rain cause most rapid and maximum dissemination. Bacteria survives in infected plant parts and spreads through rain splashes and wind. Disease is rapid during rainy days.
label: DISEASE

description: Pathogen causes  , tip  , graft union blight, twig blight, seedling rot, wood stain, stem-end rot, black root rot, fruit rot, dry rot, and brown rot of panicle. Disease is most conspicuous during October-November. It's characterized by drying back of twigs from top downwards, particularly in older trees, followed by drying of leaves giving appearance of fire scorch. Internal browning in wood tissue is observed when slit open along long axis. Cracks appear on branches and gum exudes before they die out.
label: DISEASE

description: Pathogens survive in plant debris which is the source of primary inoculum. High humidity and moist conditions favor disease development. The disease is most common in October-November. Environmental stress conditions predispose trees to infection.
label: DISEASE

description: Sudden dropping of leaves after seedling emergence. During prolonged rainy and humid weather, infection occurs at or below ground level with circular to irregular water-soaked patches. These patches enlarge and ultimately girdle entire base of seedlings. The disease affects young seedlings primarily.
label: DISEASE

description: Disease is soil-borne and pathogen survives in soils of orchards. Primary infection occurs by soil and secondary by conidia through rain or wind. High humidity, high soil moisture, cloudiness, and low temperatures below 24°C for few days are ideal for infection and disease development.
label: DISEASE

description: Epicarp darkens around base-pedicel. Circular black patch which under humid atmosphere causes soft rot aided by pectinolytic and cellulolytic enzymes. More portions of fruit turn black and soften. Fruits lose ascorbic acid and non-reducing sugars rapidly. This is a significant postharvest disease.
label: DISEASE

description: Fungus persists in infected plant parts which serve as source of inoculum. Relative humidity of 80% with temperature range of 25.9-31.5°C favors disease development. These warm, humid conditions are typical of postharvest storage environments.
label: DISEASE

description: On matured green fruits, small  s appear with greyish white center which later turn to bigger lesions with large number of acervuli seen as black dots. The disease also affects leaves ( s) and twigs (black spots). Disease is caused by Pestalotia mangiferae.
label: DISEASE

description: Temperature between 20-25°C enhances mycelial growth with sporulation taking place at pH 5.5-6.0. Wounding leads to more disease incidence. The pathogen is opportunistic, requiring injury to establish infection.
label: DISEASE

description: Symptoms noticeable only on old leaves. Initially, lesions are angular, minute, irregular, yellow to light brown, scattered over leaf lamina. As lesions enlarge, color changes from brown to cinnamon and they become almost irregular. Fully developed spots characterized by dark margins and dull grey necrotic centers. In severe infection, spots coalesce forming patches measuring 3.5-13cm in size, resulting in complete withering and defoliation of infected leaves.
label: DISEASE

description: Pathogen is seed-borne fungus and inoculum present in seeds is source of primary infection. Fungus also survives on glumes, fruit, and plant debris. Rainy seasons favor disease development. Seed treatment and debris management are important control measures.
label: DISEASE

description: fungus attacks leaves, panicles, blossoms, twigs, bark of stems, and mango fruits. Spots are circular, slightly angular, elongated, 2-4mm in diameter, brown. On young fruits, infection is grey to greyish brown with dark irregular margins. As fruit attains size, spots enlarge and center may become covered with crack fissure and corky tissues.
label: DISEASE

description: Pathogen survives in form of resting spores in soil debris. Suitable temperatures and moisture promote release of Elsinoe mangiferae spores. This cycle of secondary infections continues throughout summer until leaves and fruit fall from tree at onset of winter.
label: DISEASE

description: caused by algae causes reduction in photosynthetic activity and defoliation of leaves. Disease easily recognized by rusty red spots mainly on leaves and sometimes on petioles and bark of young twigs; it's epiphytic in nature. Spots are greenish grey and velvety in texture. Later, they turn reddish brown. Circular and slightly elevated spots sometimes coalesce to form larger and irregular spots.
label: DISEASE

description: Disease is common in closed plantations. High humidity favors development of fruiting bodies. Pathogens reproduce and survive in spots on leaves or stems and in fallen plant host debris. Frequent rains and warm weather are favorable conditions. For hosts, poor plant nutrition, poor soil drainage, and stagnant air are predisposing factors to algal infection.
label: DISEASE

description: Discrete and discolored areas all over fruit. These areas turn dark brown to black at maturity. Black fruit bodies appear on spots. Disease is caused by Phomopsis mangiferae and is soil-borne, with conidia transmitted by wind and rain water.
label: DISEASE

description: is caused by Colletotrichum species. The most important is C. asianum, a mango biotype reported in Australia, Brazil, Florida, Ghana, Mexico, Panama, Philippines, South Africa, and Thailand. Other species in the C. gloeosporioides complex (22 species total) include C. fructicola, C. gloeosporioides, C. queenslandicum, C. theobromicola, and C. tropicale. Secondary roles are played by C. acutatum complex (C. fioriniae, C. simmondsii), C. boninense complex (C. cliviae, C. karstii), and C. siamense complex species.
label: DISEASE

description: Lasiodiplodia theobromae is the most common and widespread pathogen. Other important pathogens include L. pseudotheobromae, Neofusicoccum parvum, N. mangiferae, Botryosphaeria dothidea, Neoscytalidium hyalinum, Dothiorella dominicana, D. mangiferae, Phomopsis mangiferae, and Pestalotiopsis mangiferae. Infection occurs before harvest through endophytic colonization of pedicel tissues from previous growth flushes. The disease produces heavy losses during fruit storage.
label: DISEASE

description: or black spot is caused by Alternaria alternata. It appears as black spots on fruits, alternaria leaf spots, and lesions on inflorescences. The disease is most prevalent in arid environments. In Israel, it's more important on fruit than leaves. The fungus is cosmopolitan with many host plants but effects on mango are strongest in dry conditions. It has been reported in Australia, Egypt, India, Israel, and South Africa.
label: DISEASE

description: Three genetically distinct groups cause  : Group I (Africa, Europe, Asia) is Xanthomonas citri pv. mangiferaeindicae; Group II (Brazil) is X. axonopodis pv. anacardii; Group III (French West Indies) is X. axonopodis pv. spondiae. The disease is widespread in Asia (Japan, India, Malaysia, Thailand, Philippines), Australia, UAE, Indian Ocean islands, and East/Southern Africa. It's also known as bacterial canker in India and can be the most important disease where other fungal diseases are well managed.
label: DISEASE

description: s are diverse saprophytic fungi that develop on honeydew secreted by insects like aphids, mealybugs, and scales. Black mildews are caused by tropical obligate plant pathogens, especially Meliola mangiferae. Sooty blotch refers to diseases not associated with honeydew, caused by several dothidiomycete groups. All produce dark, superficial growths on stems, leaves, and fruits. While   itself doesn't directly damage plants, heavy coating reduces photosynthesis and fruit quality.
label: DISEASE

description: is one of the most destructive mango diseases, first described in India in 1891. Trees usually aren't killed, but the vegetative phase affects canopy development and flower infection dramatically reduces fruit yield. It's widely distributed worldwide and continues spreading to disease-free areas. The disease has been reported in Australia, Brazil, Myanmar, China, Egypt, El Salvador, India, Israel, Malaysia, Mexico, Nicaragua, Oman, Pakistan, Senegal, South Africa, Sri Lanka, Sudan, Spain, Swaziland, Uganda, and the United States.
label: DISEASE

description: Fusarium mangiferae is the primary agent, reported from Australia, China, Egypt, Florida, Israel, Malaysia, Oman, South Africa, Spain, and Sri Lanka. Additional causal species include F. mexicanum and F. pseudocircinatum in Mexico; F. sterilihyphosum in Brazil and South Africa; F. tupiense in Brazil, Senegal, and Spain; F. proliferatum in Australia, China, and Malaysia; and other described and undescribed Fusarium species in various countries. The pathogen's internal location in affected trees makes chemical control difficult.
label: DISEASE

description: is caused by the host-specific fungus Oidium mangiferae. It was first described in Brazil in 1914 and is now reported in most mango-producing regions worldwide. The disease appears as white powdery fungal growth on leaves, flowers, and young fruits, causing leaf curl, distortion, premature drop, flower browning, and failure to set fruit. It's most severe during dry weather with high humidity at night.
label: DISEASE

description: Seca was first reported in 1938 in Pernambuco, Brazil, and sudden decline in 1998 in Oman, Pakistan, and UAE - they're considered the same disease. It's a lethal fungal disease. In Brazil, Ceratocystis fimbriata is the primary cause. In Oman and Pakistan, C. manginecans is the primary agent; C. omanensis is a minor pathogen. The pathogen spreads via infected propagation materials, pruning equipment, and beetle vectors. Trees killed by the disease are significant reservoirs of vectors and pathogens.
label: DISEASE

description: Diverse biotic and abiotic factors cause decline. Main fungal pathogens are endophytes with Botryosphaeria or Botryosphaeria-like teleomorphs, especially Lasiodiplodia theobromae and Neofusicoccum parvum. Stress and wound predisposition are usually associated with symptom development. Other causes include Dothiorella dominicana, Diplodia recifiensis, Ceratocystis fimbriata, Neoscytalidium dimidiatum, Colletotrichum gloeosporioides, Phomopsis spp., and Botryosphaeria ribis. Predisposing factors include injury, insects, drought, hardpan soil, high temperatures, sun scorch, high humidity, water stress, nutritional deficiencies, frost, and physical damage.
label: DISEASE

description: Phytophthora palmivora causes multiple diseases: wilt, crown rot, root rot, and death of nursery stock in Arizona, Philippines, and Thailand; trunk damage in mature trees in Ivory Coast; fruit damage in Australia, Malaysia, and West Africa. In Spain, a Phytophthora species was isolated from wilted, chlorotic trees with sparse canopies and cracked bark. These are oomycete diseases that can cause significant damage to seedlings, nursery stocks, and mature trees, though relatively less important than foliar and floral diseases.
label: DISEASE

description: Pythium vexans (oomycete) causes   and wilt of seedlings. Symptoms include wilting foliage that initially becomes pale green but later develops necrotic patches. Roots develop wet, blackened necrosis beginning in finer roots and progressing to larger roots and root collar. Rhizoctonia solani (basidiomycete) also causes   and damping off of seedlings in India. Both pathogens can cause significant damage to young mango plants.
label: DISEASE

description: is caused by the fungus Sclerotium rolfsii (teleomorph: Athelia rolfsii). This disease has been reported in Brazil, India, and the Philippines. It's a soil-borne fungal disease that can affect mango trees. Like other soil-borne diseases, it's relatively less important than foliar and floral diseases but can cause significant damage when conditions favor its development.
label: DISEASE

description: is caused by the basidiomycete Erythricium salmonicolor (anamorph: Necator decretus). Also known as cobweb, rubellosis, and thread blight, it affects many woody plants in humid tropics and is one of the most destructive mango diseases. It significantly reduces tree vigor and yield, especially in young trees. The disease has been mainly studied on rubber (Hevea brasiliensis) in Southeast Asia. It thrives in humid tropical conditions.
label: DISEASE

description: is caused by Elsinoë mangiferae (anamorph: Sphaceloma mangiferae). First described in Cuba and Florida in the 1940s, it's now widespread in the western hemisphere.   is important in nurseries since young tissues are most susceptible. High humidity promotes infection. The disease affects young, developing tissues more severely than mature plant parts, making it a particular concern for nursery operations and young tree establishment.
label: DISEASE

description: is caused by the bacterium Pseudomonas syringae pv. syringae. Reported in Spain, Israel, Portugal, and possibly Egypt, it affects apical buds, leaves, and panicles but not fruit. Dark brown to blackish necrosis develops on vegetative floral buds and can extend from affected buds to leaf petioles. In high damage conditions, it can kill large portions of the canopy and much of the tree's bloom, significantly impacting productivity.
label: DISEASE

description: is caused by the fungus Macrophoma mangiferae (Ascomycota). It has been reported in India and Nigeria and detected in shipments to the USA from Mexico, though it doesn't seem to be a serious problem. The disease affects mango foliage but is not considered a major threat to mango production. It represents one of several minor foliar diseases that can occur on mango under certain conditions.
label: DISEASE

description: is caused by Pestalotiopsis mangiferae (synonym: Pestalolia mangiferae), which also causes stem-end rot. It's a weak pathogen that usually requires wounding to infect mango. The disease is usually unimportant and occurs mainly on unhealthy or poorly maintained trees. The fungus produces abundant conidia in acervuli that develop in   lesions and necrotic areas on fruit. Other Pestalotiopsis species affecting mango include P. mangifolia and P. versicolor.
label: DISEASE

description: , also known as red rust, is caused by the alga Cephaleuros virescens and less frequently by C. parasiticus (family Trentepohliaceae, division Chlorophyta). This is an algal infection rather than a fungal disease. It appears as rust-colored spots on leaves. While not typically devastating, it can affect tree appearance and in severe cases may impact photosynthesis. It's more common in humid environments where algae can thrive on leaf surfaces.
label: DISEASE

description: is caused by Phoma glomerata and is widespread in India. It occurs only on old leaves. Initially, lesions are minute and yellow-brown. As they expand, they darken to brown or cinnamon, become irregular, and may develop dark margins and dull-grey centers. In severe cases, necrotic patches as large as 13 cm in diameter may develop, causing defoliation. This disease specifically targets older foliage rather than young, developing tissues.
label: DISEASE

description: is caused by Phoma sorghina and is present in India. On young leaves, it causes irregular to roughly circular, water-soaked spots up to 2.5mm in diameter. Lesions are brown with yellow to brown margins. Lesions on midribs are elongated and more conspicuous and may coalesce to up to 14cm in diameter. The symptoms can be confused with those caused by anthracnose. Unlike phoma blight which affects old leaves, this disease targets young foliage.
label: DISEASE

description: disorders are caused by Fusarium decemcellulare (synonym: F. rigidiuscula). These are usually minor problems but can cause general loss of vigor. The disease has been reported in Florida (USA), Mexico, and Venezuela. While not typically devastating, these disorders can affect tree health over time, particularly when trees are under other stresses or in suboptimal growing conditions.
label: DISEASE

description: is a relatively unimportant disease affecting mango leaves and branches. The causal fungus is Rhinocladium corticola (teleomorph: Peziotrichum corticolum), described on the bark of trees in Poona, India. While not a major threat to mango production, it can occur under certain conditions and may contribute to overall tree stress when combined with other factors.
label: DISEASE

description: is caused by Verticillium dahliae (originally attributed to V. albo-atrum). The disease was first reported in Florida. It's a soil-borne fungal disease that can affect mango trees, causing wilting symptoms due to vascular infection. Like other soil-borne diseases of mango, it's relatively less important than foliar and floral diseases but can cause problems in affected trees.
label: DISEASE

description: is caused by Rigidoporus lignosus, a basidiomycete common in soils of humid tropics of Africa and Asia. More recently, Rosellinia necatrix was reported as the causal agent of white root rot in mango trees in Spain. These are soil-borne fungal pathogens that attack the root system, potentially causing significant damage to affected trees in areas where they occur.
label: DISEASE

description: appears as dark brown to black lesions on leaves, stems, flowers, and fruits. On fruits, it causes dark, sunken spots that can merge and lead to fruit rot. On leaves, you'll see irregular brown spots with dark margins. The disease is most severe during warm, humid conditions and can cause significant yield loss if not managed properly.
label: DISEASE

description: manifests as dark, sunken lesions on branches and trunks, often with gum exudation. On leaves, you'll see water-soaked spots that turn brown or black. Infected branches may show dieback, and the disease can spread rapidly during wet, warm weather. The cankers can girdle branches, leading to wilting and death of affected parts.
label: DISEASE

description: damage appears as clean, circular cuts on leaf margins and young shoots. You'll notice leaves with semicircular notches along the edges, resembling someone cut them with scissors. The adult weevils feed at night, so you may not see them during the day. Severe infestations can lead to defoliation and stunted growth of young trees.
label: PEST

description: disease shows as progressive wilting and drying of shoots from tip downwards. You'll see browning of young twigs and branches, starting at the tips and moving toward the main stem. Leaves turn brown, dry up, and remain attached to dead branches. The disease often occurs during flowering and fruiting stages, causing significant yield reduction.
label: DISEASE

description: infestation causes abnormal swellings or galls on leaves, flowers, and young shoots. On leaves, you'll see conical or pouch-like galls on the upper surface. Infested panicles show distorted flowers and reduced fruit set. The galls appear as reddish or greenish protrusions and contain tiny larvae inside. Heavy infestations can cause premature leaf drop and significant flower damage.
label: PEST

description: appears as white, powdery fungal growth on leaves, flowers, and young fruits. You'll see a dusty white coating on the upper and lower leaf surfaces, panicles, and young shoots. Infected leaves may curl, become distorted, and drop prematurely. On flowers, the disease causes browning and failure to set fruit. The disease is most severe during dry weather with high humidity at night.
label: DISEASE

description: appears as black, velvety fungal growth on leaves, branches, and fruits. The black coating covers the leaf surface, reducing photosynthesis and making the tree look dirty. This mould grows on honeydew secreted by sucking insects like scales, mealybugs, and aphids. While the mould itself doesn't directly damage the plant, heavy coating can reduce fruit quality and tree vigor.
label: DISEASE

description: Fruit fly damage appears as small puncture marks on the fruit surface where females have laid eggs. You'll notice soft, sunken spots that may ooze liquid. Internally, the fruit flesh shows tunneling and rot caused by feeding larvae. Infested fruits often drop prematurely or ripen unevenly. Cut open suspect fruits to look for white maggots inside the pulp.
label: PEST

description: damage is often difficult to detect externally. You may see small oviposition scars on young fruits. As fruits mature, infested ones may drop prematurely or show uneven ripening. Cut open suspect fruits to find larvae or pupae inside the seed. The seed becomes hollow, brown, and filled with frass. Adult emergence holes appear as circular openings in mature or stored fruits.
label: PEST

description: attack mangoes from young fruit stage through ripening. You'll see entry holes on the fruit surface with frass around them.
