Internally, larvae tunnel through the pulp causing extensive damage and rot. Infested fruits often drop prematurely. The attack begins when fruits are 60 days after flowering and can continue until harvest. Damaged fruits become unmarketable and susceptible to secondary infections.
label: PEST

description: Look for small circular holes in the trunk and branches with sawdust-like frass around them. You may see resin or gum oozing from entry points. Infested branches show wilting, yellowing, or dieback. Tunnels inside the wood weaken structural integrity. Heavy infestations can cause branch breakage or tree death. Adult beetles may be visible attempting to bore into bark during their active season.
label: PEST

description: Leafhoppers feed on young leaves, shoots, and flower panicles by sucking sap. You'll see yellowing, curling, and browning of leaf tips and edges. Infested panicles show poor flower development and reduced fruit set. Severe infestations cause leaf drop and stunted growth. Hoppers excrete honeydew that encourages sooty mould growth. The damage is most critical during flowering and early fruit development stages.
label: PEST

description: Scales appear as small, immobile bumps on leaves, twigs, and branches. You'll see white, brown, or pink waxy coverings depending on the species. Heavy infestations cause yellowing leaves, stunted growth, and dieback. Scales excrete honeydew that leads to sooty mould growth, giving the tree a black, dirty appearance. Infestations often become serious following insecticide use against other pests.
label: PEST

description: Midge larvae feed inside flower buds and young panicles, causing gall formation and distortion. Infested flowers fail to open properly or drop prematurely. You'll see deformed panicles with swollen, discolored tissue. The tiny larvae are inside the galls. Severe infestations drastically reduce fruit set and yield. Midges can also cause galls on leaves and young twigs beyond just flowers.
label: PEST

description: Caterpillars feed on flower buds, open flowers, and young panicles. You'll see holes in petals, webbing on panicles, and frass on flowers. Severe infestations can completely defoliate panicles, preventing fruit set. Some species like Cryptoblades gnidiella web leaves and flowers together. The damage occurs during the critical flowering period, directly impacting yield. Constant monitoring is necessary to prevent significant damage.
label: PEST

description: Throughout the year there is a low population of hoppers, but it spikes in February-April and June-August. Their multiplication is aided by the presence of shade and high humidity. Such conditions are common in orchards that are old, neglected, and densely planted. Hoppers are the most damaging and prevalent of all mango pests, with tender plant parts being punctured and sap sucked by large numbers of nymphs and adult hoppers.
label: PEST

description: After copulation, the female crawls down the tree in April-May to deposit eggs in great numbers covered with white egg sacs in crevices in the soil. Until November or December, the eggs are in the diapause stage in the soil. The tiny newly hatched nymphs climb up the tree shortly after hatching. They begin sucking sap of delicate plant parts after crawling up the tree. Nymphs and adults suck sap, lowering the plant's vitality, and produce honeydew which promotes sooty mold growth.
label: PEST

description: The midge damages crops in three stages. The first attack occurs when floral buds burst, followed by fruit set and tender new leaves. The most destructive attack is the first, which destroys the entire inflorescence before flowering and fruiting. Flies deposit eggs on inflorescence. Minute maggots penetrate tender parts and feed after hatching. Floral parts eventually dry and fall off. Between January and March, there are three to four overlapping generations. Mature larvae go into diapause in soil during unfavorable weather, ending diapause in January.
label: PEST

description: The emergence of fruit flies begins in April, with the highest population recorded between May and July, which coincides with fruit maturity. The oriental   is one of the most serious pests of mango in the country, causing problems with fresh fruit exports. The most common fruit flies are Bactrocera dorsalis and B. zonata. The female uses pointed ovipositor to puncture outer wall of mature fruits and insert eggs in small clusters inside mesocarp.
label: PEST

description: This pest is more likely to attack old, shady, and neglected orchards. Larvae of this moth feed on the bark. The caterpillar spins a brown silken web on the tree which consists of its excreta and wood particles. Larvae also make shelter tunnels inside the stem in which they rest. Larvae feed from April to December. There is only one generation in a year.
label: PEST

description: This beetle's grub feeds inside stems, boring upward, causing branches to dry out. Eggs are laid either in slits of tree trunk or in cavities in main branches and stems, covered with viscous fluid. Pupation takes place within the stem. In July and August, beetles emerge. There is only one generation of the pest in a year.
label: PEST

description: It is a major pest of mangoes in many parts of India, particularly the Terai region of Uttar Pradesh, north Bihar, and West Bengal. This pest creates green conical galls in leaf axis. Activity starts in August. Galls dry out after emergence of psyllid adults in March. Females lay eggs in midribs and lateral axis of new leaves. There is only one generation in a year.
label: PEST

description: This is a major pest that affects the export and processing industry. A female lays eggs on epicarp of partially developed fruits or under rind of ripening fruits. Newly emerged grubs bore through pulp, feed on seed coat, and later cause damage to cotyledons. Pupation takes place inside the seed. Discoloration of pulp adjacent to affected portion has been observed. There is only one generation in a year.
label: PEST

description: Infestation starts with new flushes and panicle emergence during 13th to 22nd standard meteorological weeks (second week of March to last week of May) in northern plains.   have created havoc in most mango-growing areas.   caused approximately half of fruit damage in severely affected orchards. Larval and adult stages are damaging stages.
label: PEST

description: Damage to young leaves, growing buds, inflorescence, flowers, immature and developing fruits occurs by lacerating and sucking sap from tissues. This causes silvery or brown patches on affected parts where plant cells have been destroyed. Curling up of leaves and wilting of inflorescences occur. In severe cases, affected fruits become rusty in appearance. This pest can damage entire new growth if not treated properly.
label: PEST

description: The   affects both mesocarp as well as seeds. Young larvae scrape the epidermal tissue and mature ones bore into fruit and feed on pulp. Affected fruits exude resin and black or brown rough sticky patches can be seen in infected areas. This damage reduces fruit quality and marketability.
label: PEST

description: This pest has become a serious and emerging problem as one of most obnoxious pests in northern states. Old orchards with less space between tree canopies harbour more insects than open orchards. Infestation begins in April and lasts until December. Initially, caterpillars feed on leaf surface by scraping. Later they make web of tender shoots and leaves together and feed within them. Infestation is severe in shady conditions.
label: PEST

description: Larvae enter the mid rib of leaves and then enter into young shoots through growing points by tunneling downwards. They excrete their excreta through the entrance hole and the shoot becomes hollow. Larvae bore into young shoots, resulting in drooping of leaves and wilting of shoots. Larvae also bore into inflorescence stalk.
label: PEST

description: Almost a dozen insect pests damage the crop to significant extent, causing severe losses, classified as major pests of mango. These include hopper, mealybug, inflorescence midge, fruit fly, scale insect, shoot borer, leaf webber, and stone weevil. Insects that infest the crop during flowering and fruiting periods cause most severe damage. The hopper is considered the most damaging and prevalent of all mango pests.
label: PEST

description: results from interaction between sap-feeding insects (like aphids and scale) and non-parasitic fungi (Meliola mangiferae). The insects produce honeydew which acts as food for fungi, causing black growth on plant surfaces.
label: DISEASE

description: reduces gas exchange and photosynthesis by forming a black layer on leaf surfaces. It develops as a result of honeydew secretion from sap-feeding insects, which fungi use as food substrate.
label: DISEASE

description: White superficial fungal growth appears on leaves, fruits, panicle stalks and flowers. The fungus Oidium mangiferae thrives in high humidity and moderate temperatures.
label: DISEASE

description: Tiny soft-bodied insects (brownish, greyish to blackish) suck fluid from young leaves. They produce honeydew that encourages sooty mould growth, inhibiting photosynthesis.
label: PEST

description: Stationary shell-like oval, flat or pear-shaped insects that appear as protective scales on plant surfaces. They suck sap causing direct biomass and water loss.
label: PEST

description: Caused by Colletotrichum gloeosporioides and Glomerella cingulata (sexual stage). The fungus survives saprophytically on dead branches and plant debris.
label: DISEASE

description: Tiny insects that infest buds, shoots, leaves and fruits. Adults are dark with long antennae. Larvae mine leaves causing galls or swellings.
label: PEST

description: Caused by Elsinoe mangiferae or Denticularia mangiferae fungi. Lesions can be confused with anthracnose but have distinct corky, cracked appearance.
label: DISEASE

description: Oval-shaped adults with dark brown mottled markings. Females pierce fruit to lay eggs; larvae burrow through pulp to seeds, causing fruit drop and decay. It's a quarantine pest.
label: PEST

description: Irregular brown to black necrotic patches on leaves, twigs, stems, branches and fruits. Fruits show water-soaked spots that erupt producing exudates. Cankerous lesions release gummy ooze containing bacteria.
label: DISEASE

description: Small (2-3 mm) white waxy-bodied insects resembling cotton wool. They produce sugary honeydew that attracts ants and protects them from natural enemies.
label: PEST

description: Caused by Lasiodiplodia theobromae or Colletotrichum species. Characterized by elongated black necrotic areas on twigs with death progressing from tip downwards.
label: DISEASE

description: Ceratitis cosyra, Bactrocera obliqua, Bactrocera frauenfeldi, and Anastrepha species. Females puncture fruit to lay eggs; larvae feed internally causing fruit drop.
label: PEST

description: Irregular flat or pear-shaped, tough, white or dirty white scales on leaves, branches and fruits. Eggs hatch into crawlers that move to feeding sites.
label: PEST

description: Interveinal chlorosis and marginal necrosis, dieback of young stems, eventual tree death. Gummosis appears on necrotic tissue over time.
label: DISEASE

description: Adults have yellow and dark brown marks. They feed on pollen and nectar from panicles but don't cause significant economic damage.
label: PEST

description: Water-soaked lesions on leaves that become sunken. Caused by Xanthomonas axonopodis pv. Mangiferaeindicae.
label: DISEASE

description: White to colourless insects make tunnels in branches, feed on plant tissue, form soil mounds, and disrupt food/water movement. Common in older trees.
label: PEST

description: Cracks on stems and branches leading to bark rupture followed by resin exudation. Different from bacterial   which has distinct bacterial ooze.
label: DISEASE

description: appears as whitish grey mycelial wefts initially on inflorescence (flowers and flower buds). The fungus spreads to tender fruits, leaves and shoots, covering the entire surface with a powdery substance consisting of millions of spores (conidia) borne in chains. On young fruits, the entire surface becomes covered by mildew, and as fruit grows, the epidermis cracks and corky tissues form with purplish brown blotchy areas. On young leaves, small irregular greyish patches appear mostly on the underside, which coalesce and turn purplish brown under favorable conditions.
label: DISEASE

description: On leaves,   appears as oval or irregular vinaceous brown to deep brown spots of variable size scattered over the leaf surface. Under damp conditions, elongated brown necrotic areas measuring 20-25 mm in diameter form, which later get blighted and rupture, showing a 'shot hole' appearance. On fruits, small water-soaked lesions develop that turn dark brown to black. Initially spots are round but after coalescence form large irregular blotches or cover the entire fruit. The spots have large deep cracks that penetrate deep into the fruit causing extensive rotting. Under moist conditions, blackened areas become covered with minute pinkish reproductive bodies.
label: DISEASE

description: Blossom blight is the most destructive phase of   as it affects fruit set and yield. Blackish brown specks appear on peduncles and flowers which gradually enlarge and coalesce to cause death of flowers. The infected flowers fall off, leaving persistent spikes on the peduncles. Continuous wet weather during flowering causes serious blossom blight.
label: DISEASE

description: Small water-soaked lesions appear in groups on the leaf surface, which increase in size, turn brown to black and get surrounded by a yellowish halo. Several lesions may coalesce to form large necrotic patches which are often rough and raised. On young fruits, water-soaked lesions develop that turn dark brown to black. Infected fruits may show cracks in the skin and badly affected ones drop prematurely. Under natural conditions, the pathogen causes water-soaked spots which turn into cankers on fruits, leaves, petioles, twigs and branches.
label: DISEASE

description: The disease is characterized by dying back of twigs from top downwards with drying of leaves, particularly in older trees, followed by complete defoliation giving a fire scorch appearance. Discoloration and darkening of bark on young twigs at a certain distance from the tip is external evidence. Upper leaves lose green color and gradually turn brown with upward folding of margins. Such leaves shrivel and fall off in a month, leaving shrivelled twigs bare. Internal browning in wood tissue is observed on splitting open the twigs along the long axis. The disease is most conspicuous during October and November.
label: DISEASE

description: The disease is characterized by presence of a black velvety thin membranous covering on the leaf surface. In severe cases, the tree appears black due to heavy infestation of moulds on entire surface of leaves and twigs. Affected leaves curl and shrivel under dry conditions. The foliage appears black, ugly with masses of black spores that adhere to leaf surface due to sticky 'honey dew', hence the name ' '. Severity depends upon sugary secretion by insects like mango hopper, scales, coccids and mealy bugs. During flowering, if fungus infects blossoms, fruit setting is affected and small fruits may fall.
label: DISEASE

description: Bunchy top phase appears on young plants in nursery beds when they are 4-5 months old. The characteristic symptom is formation of a bunch or occasionally several bunches at the top or a little lower down the main shoot. The bunch is formed of numerous thickened small shootlets, clustered together and arising from a leaf axil, on which are borne many small rudimentary leaves. These shootlets are much thicker than the main axis from which they arise. Growth of the plant is stopped, giving a 'Bunchy top' appearance.
label: DISEASE

description: The most characteristic symptom is reduction in length of the primary axis and secondary branches of the panicle which makes flowers appear in clusters. Frequently, flower buds are transformed into vegetative buds and large numbers of small leaves and stems with appreciably reduced internodes are compacted together, giving a witches broom-like appearance. In other cases, flower buds seldom open and remain as dull, green unopened buds. The main axis is shortened but flowers are changed into small leaves. Malformed panicles normally do not bear fruits. Even fruits set in the season do not grow more than pea size. The malformed heads dry up in black masses and persist on the tree for a long time, even until next flowering season.
label: DISEASE

description: The disease is characterized by presence of profuse gumming on the surface of affected wood and bark of trunk and larger branches, more common at branch cracks. In severe cases, droplets of gum trickle down on stem, and bark turns dark brown with longitudinal cracks. Bark rots and the tree dries up because of girdling effects. Recent surveys show 30-40% of young mango trees are affected especially in sandy soil. The disease occurs on stems and branches of seedling as well as grafted trees and is noticed after rainy season towards winter.
label: DISEASE

description: The disease is readily recognized by presence of rusty red fructifications of the alga on surface of leaves, veins, petioles and young twigs. Initially spots are greenish grey in color and velvety in texture, finally turning reddish brown. Spots are circular to irregular in shape, erumpent, measuring 2 mm in diameter but when coalesce may reach up to 1 cm. After shedding of spores, the algal matrix remains attached to leaf surface, leaving a creamy white mark at the original rust spot. The disease can cause reduction in photosynthetic activity and defoliation which results in lowering the vitality of plants.
label: DISEASE

description: is characterized by presence of brown spots on leaf lamina. These spots may develop from margins or tip. Initially, spots are brown and minute which gradually increase in size and become dark brown. Some spots form large lesions, with greyish white center and tan colored margins. At this stage, black spots of acervuli may become visible to naked eye in the central region, more on upper surface of leaf and never extend beyond midrib. Small brown spots also appear on green mature fruits which gradually increase in size, become dark brown with greyish white center and black dots of acervuli appear. Fruits drop off when disease advances to stalk end. Moist atmosphere helps in increasing and hastening infection.
label: DISEASE

description: The disease is noticed as pinkish powdery coating on twigs and branches. Later, the fungus invades bark to get established in internal tissues and interferes with transport of nutrients. Often fungal growth spreads to girdle the stem. Severely infected bark gets shredded and wood is exposed. Leaves turn yellow and dry. Roots are not infected. The pink color on tissues represents profuse conidial production by the fungus, hence the name ' '. Also known as 'thread blight', rubellosis or cobweb. The disease is widespread in many tropical and subtropical regions.
label: DISEASE

description: The disease is characterized by presence of mycelial weft on base of stem at ground level. Beneath mycelial growth, a dark brown spot may develop which gradually encircles the base of stem. At this stage, the succulent top droops and bends towards ground, tissues lose turgidity and seedling dies within a week. When disease is at peak, fungus may be seen encircling the stem up to 2 inches or more above ground level. The disease also causes severe rotting of seeds during or before germination. Sclerotia are pin head size, initially white, but at maturity chocolate brown in color measuring 1.0-2.6 mm in diameter.
label: DISEASE

description: The disease is characterized by sudden drooping of leaves after emergence of seedlings from soil. During prolonged rainy and humid weather, infection occurs at/or below ground level with circular to irregular water-soaked patches. These patches enlarge and ultimately girdle entire base of stem. On account of rotting, diseased tissues become soft, dark brown or black and entire seedling collapses and dies. Fungal mycelia and sclerotia are densely present on severely infected parts. Rotting may spread both above and below the stem, down to roots, and infected roots are disintegrated.
label: DISEASE

description: The disease is characterized by presence of yellowish pinhead spots on leaves, twigs and rarely on stems. Soon after, spots enlarge and become light to dark brown in color. Later, these spots become oval to irregular in shape, raised and dark purplish. Tissues become ash colored due to appearance of pycnidia on surface of lamina. Due to complete drying of leaf, infection travels downwards towards petiole. The bark of infected stem/twig turns grey because of appearance of elliptical lesions. The disease has been found present throughout the year in Delhi and other parts of India with heavy incidence during rainy season (July-September).
label: DISEASE

description: The disease is very common in Bijnore (U.P.) and Malda (West Bengal) on old trees. Younger trees less than 5-6 years are not affected. Unlike gummosis,   is characterized by development of deep longitudinal cracks in main branches of tree trunk, but without much exudation, measuring 15-40 cm in length. Rotting is not associated with cracks but underlying wood is severely pitted. Gum pockets are also noticed along with cracks. Later, bark gets dried and pulled off resulting in girdling effects such as yellowing and shedding of leaves and die back of branches. These symptoms have been noticed in cvs. Fazli, Himsagar, Lakhan Bhog, Ashina, Kuwan Pahar, Dashehari and Bombay Green.
label: DISEASE

description: Since the description of the perfect stage of the pathogen has not been given, the conidial stage is known as Oidium mangiferae Berthet. The pathogen is not reported on hosts other than mango. Mildew pathogen persists on infected leaves of previous year's flush which are retained on plant in succeeding year. Abundant conidia are produced and blown over to new flushes and provide sufficient spore load for initiating disease. Fresh infection on young leaves in first week of December (when flowers are not present) confirms the fungus perpetuates in asexual form on leaves of mango.
label: DISEASE

description: The disease is caused by Colletotrichum gloeosporioides Penz. (=Glomerella cingulata (Stons.) Spauld & Schrenk). Seven species of Colletotrichum are known to cause fruit rot in Queensland. It was found desirable to designate a new form as Glomerella cingulata var. minor. The conidial state causes   on mango, papaya, avocado, apple and other hosts in Queensland. Colletotrichum acutatum has been reported from New South Wales and India, isolated from leaves, panicles and fruits. Twig blight phase is caused by Gloeosporium mangiferae P. Henn but it is identical to C. gloeosporioides. Six new species of Colletotrichum including C. mangiferae on mango were also reported.
label: DISEASE

description: The disease is caused by Xanthomonas campestris pv. mangiferaeindicae (Patel et al.) Robbs et al. It is a gram negative rod, motile by monotrichous flagella and 3 to 4 pathotypes have been identified. The bacterium survives in infected plant parts on the tree and in resident form on weed hosts and mango leaves and fruits. It survives up to 8 months in diseased leaves. The pathogen was found pathogenic on several hosts. The bacterium enters into mango leaves through stomata, through stomata and lenticels in fruits, and through lenticels in twigs. It is an exclusively intercellular parenchymatous pathogen.
label: DISEASE

description: In India,   of mango is caused by Botryodiplodia theobromae Pat. In U.S.A. (California) twig blight of mango was associated with Botryosphaeria ribis. In Florida, tip die-back has been reported and they isolated the conidial stage of Botryosphaeria ribis. Other causal agents include Physalospora rhodina and Ceratocystis fimbriata associated with same type of die-back. Botryodiplodia theobromae is an aggressive and vigorous pathogen able to infect exceptionally large number of host plants, causing root rot, fruit rot, dry rot, wood stain, die-back, stem end rot, seedling rot, graft union blight, twig blight and brown rot of panicle.
label: DISEASE

description: Recent findings demonstrate that disease may be of fungal origin. Fusarium moniliforme Sheld. was reported for first time, associated with bodies similar to chlamydospores, particularly in cortex when inoculated with spore suspension. Cross inoculation studies with strains of F. moniliforme confirmed host specificity and mango strains only caused typical disease symptoms. Fusarium oxysporum was shown to be involved in causing malformation and fungus was isolated from all parts of plants. It is just possible that disease is caused by more than one species of Fusarium. The fungus was further identified as F. moniliforme var. subglutinans. Although fungus does not sporulate in situ, it does so on drying malformed panicles.
label: DISEASE

description: is caused by several fungi including Meliola mangiferae Earle, Capnodium mangiferae Cke. and Brown, Capnodium ramosum (Cke.) Tripospermum acerinum (Syd.) Speg. The disease is also caused by Microxyphium columnatum, Leptoxyphium fumago and Tripospermum myrti. The mycelium of fungi is superficial and does not penetrate the host tissue. The fungi involved, in true sense, are non-pathogenic, because these do not either enter host tissue or absorb nutrients. They draw their nutrition not from host, but from sweet 'honey dew' secreted by insects. Damage by fungi is not direct but indirect, as they interfere with normal functioning of plant by cutting off effective leaf area for photosynthesis.
label: DISEASE

description: The disease is caused by the alga Cephaleuros virescens Kunze (Syn. C. parasiticus Karst, C. mycoidea Karst). The thallus is a pseudo-parenchymatous tissue, one to several cells in thickness, in which cells are arranged radially. Rain water has been found to be a source for spread of alga and infection increases during rainy season. Maximum temperature of 30°C, minimum temperature around 25°C with high RH and frequent moderate rains with high wind velocity are conducive for growth and spread of this algal pathogen.
label: DISEASE

description: larvae roll and tie the tender apical leaves using silky threads and feed inside. Rolled leaves, faecal matter on lower leaves, and damaged tender shoots are clear signs of attack.
label: PEST

description: The grown-up   larva is greenish-brown in colour with a black head and dark round spots on the body. It grows up to 2.4–2.6 cm long.
label: PEST

description: Young caterpillars scrape chlorophyll leaving mesh-like dry leaves. Grown-up larvae eat entire leaves, leaving branches almost leafless.
label: PEST

description: The mature larva is reddish brown with a black head and long thick hairs. It grows up to 4–5.5 cm in length.
label: PEST

description: larvae cut young shoots near the base, causing plants to fall or dry suddenly, especially at night.
label: PEST

description: larva is stout, pale greenish brown with dark markings and grey-yellow stripes. It grows 3.5–4 cm long.
label: PEST

description: s create irregular holes and notches on leaves by feeding from the middle of the leaf.
label: PEST

description: are insects that eat mulberry leaves and reduce leaf yield. Major   are leaf roller, Bihar hairy caterpillar, cutworm and wingless grasshopper.
label: PEST

description: attack is identified by holes on stems or branches, sawdust-like frass near the holes, tunnel formation inside stems, and withering followed by drying of affected branches.
label: PEST

description: Adult  s are large, elongated dark grey beetles (4–6 cm long) with very long antennae. The grubs live inside stems and branches.
label: PEST

description: Termite attack is identified by earthen sheaths on stems, subterranean mud galleries on soil, earthen mounds near plants, and bark feeding damage.
label: PEST

description: Plants show sudden wilting, branches become leafless, and entire plants may dry due to root damage by white grubs living underground.
label: PEST

description: White grub is the larval stage of  . It lives in soil and feeds on mulberry roots causing plant drying.
label: PEST

description: are pests that damage roots and stems causing drying of plants. Major pests are stem borer, termites, and cockchafer beetle.
label: PEST

description: appears as brown, irregular necrotic spots on leaves. Spots enlarge and merge to form 'shot holes'. In severe cases, leaves turn yellow and fall.
label: DISEASE

description: shows white powdery patches on the lower leaf surface and yellow chlorotic patches on the upper surface. Severe infection turns patches brown-black.
label: DISEASE

description: shows small circular brown eruptive spots on leaves that later cause yellowing and drying of mature leaves.
label: DISEASE

description: forms a thick black coating on the upper surface of mulberry leaves, reducing photosynthesis and leaf quality.
label: DISEASE

description: Affected plants show stunted growth, yellowing of leaf margins, low moisture in leaves, and knots or galls on roots. Roots have spherical swellings of different sizes.
label: DISEASE

description: Sudden withering of plants, yellowing and dropping of leaves from bottom to top, and weak regrowth after pruning are common symptoms.
label: DISEASE

description: Roots show rotting of cortex, blackening due to fungal growth, poor anchorage in soil, and severe plants can be easily uprooted.
label: DISEASE

description: Leaf rolling and tying of mulberry leaves is caused by leaf roller larvae. They bind leaf edges with silk and feed from inside the rolled leaf.
label: PEST

description: Leaves appear rolled, stitched with silk threads, and chewed from inside. Faecal pellets may be seen on lower leaves.
label: PEST

description: Young  s feed gregariously on leaf tissue, leaving veins intact, giving a mesh-like appearance.
label: PEST

description: Leaves are skeletonized in early stages, and severe attack leads to complete defoliation of branches.
label: PEST

description: causes bunchy top appearance of apical shoots due to leaf curling, shortened internodes, thickened stems, and presence of white cotton-like masses. This condition is called Tukra.
label: PEST

description: causes leaf yellowing, curling, premature leaf drop, stunted growth, honeydew secretion, black sooty mould, and presence of red or black ants.
label: PEST

description: Thrips cause white streaks that turn into silvery blotches with black faecal spots on leaf underside. Later patches turn brown and leaves curl and fall.
label: PEST

description: This thrips species causes silvery or brown patches on leaves, leaf curling, and stunted plant growth similar to P. mori damage.
label: PEST

description: Eggs are laid in spiral waxy patterns on leaf underside. Leaves show curling, yellowing, honeydew, white waxy dust, and black sooty mould growth.
label: PEST

description: Snails make circular holes in tender leaves and scrape bark on tender stems. Leaves may have slime (mucus) trails and plants show stunted growth.
label: PEST

description: s are nocturnal. They hide under leaves, bark, or stones during the day and come out at night to feed.
label: PEST

description: s cause shot holes in leaves, leave shiny slime trails on plant parts, and scrape bark on tender stems causing shoot drying.
label: PEST

description: s peel bark superficially and may eat entire leaves leaving only petiole. They are usually detritivores but can become pests.
label: PEST

description: Leaves develop white speckles that turn into large greyish patches, with fine webbing on the underside. Affected leaves wither and dry.
label: PEST

description: Plants show stunted growth and yellowing of leaf margins. Roots develop spherical galls or knots of different sizes.
label: DISEASE

description: appears as small brown to dark circular spots on older leaves with yellow halos around them. As disease increases, spots enlarge and merge, causing leaf drying and premature leaf fall. Severe infection reduces plant vigor and yield.
label: DISEASE

description: appears as small, grey to light brown spots with dark borders on leaves. In severe cases, leaves turn yellow, dry up and fall, reducing photosynthesis and pod yield.
label: DISEASE

description: causes yellow patches on the upper surface of leaves and greyish fungal growth on the lower surface. Leaves may curl, dry and fall, reducing plant strength.
label: DISEASE

description: Leaves become curled, thickened and distorted with stunted plant growth. Infected plants show reduced flowering and small malformed pods.
label: DISEASE

description: Small round brown spots with yellow margins appear on leaves. Black tiny dots (fungal fruiting bodies) may be seen inside spots. Leaves dry prematurely under heavy infection.
label: DISEASE

description: appears as brown, irregular spots on leaves caused by C. malayensis, or sooty black, angular spots on the lower surface of leaves caused by C. abelmoschi. Both types cause severe defoliation and are common during humid season. The spots are distinctive and can lead to significant leaf loss if not managed.
label: DISEASE

description: The characteristic symptom is yellowing of the entire network of veins in the leaf blade (vein clearing). In severe infections, younger leaves turn yellow, become reduced in size, and the plant is highly stunted. Infection restricts flowering and fruits are not formed or turn smaller, harder, and rough. Loss in fruit yield ranges from 50-100% based on disease incidence.
label: DISEASE

description: appears as grayish powdery growth on both the under and upper surface of leaves. Affected leaves turn yellow and drop off, leading to severe yield loss. The disease is caused by Erysiphe cichoracearum.
label: DISEASE

description: occurs in two stages: Pre-emergence phase where seedlings are killed just before reaching soil surface with complete rotting of radical and plumule. Post-emergence phase shows infection of young collar tissues at ground level. Infected tissues become soft and water-soaked, causing seedlings to topple over or collapse.
label: DISEASE

description: shows two types of symptoms: Brown irregular spots caused by Cercospora malayensis or sooty black spots caused by C. abelmoschi. In wet conditions, the disease significantly reduces leaf area, affecting plant photosynthesis and overall vigor.
label: DISEASE

description: (YVMV) shows a characteristic yellow network pattern on leaf veins with green islands between them. As the disease progresses, entire leaves turn yellow, plants become stunted, and fruits are small and deformed, making them unmarketable.
label: DISEASE

description: (OELCV) shows distinctive pin-head sized enations (outgrowths) on the underside of leaves, giving them a warty, rough texture. Leaves curl severely, stems become twisted, and fruits are small and deformed. This disease is different from YVMV due to the characteristic enations.
label: DISEASE

description: Look for withering and drooping of tender shoots, small boreholes in fruits, and larval tunnels inside fruits. Affected fruits become unmarketable. You may also find dull-green caterpillars with black spots inside damaged shoots and fruits.
label: PEST

description: causes yellowing and curling of leaf margins, a condition called 'hopper burn'. Leaves turn rust-red, then dry and drop off. This results in reduced plant vigor and lower yields.
label: PEST

description: infestation causes leaf yellowing, drying, and curling. Plants develop sooty mold on honeydew secreted by whiteflies. Whiteflies also transmit Yellow Vein Mosaic Virus (YVMV) and Okra Enation Leaf Curl Virus (OELCV), causing severe viral diseases.
label: PEST

description: causes wilting of seedlings and older plants. Leaves turn yellow (chlorosis), vascular tissues show brown discoloration when stems are cut, plants become stunted, and eventually die. The disease can occur at any growth stage.
label: DISEASE

description: Dig up plants showing poor growth and examine roots for characteristic galls or knots. Above-ground symptoms include stunted growth, yellowing leaves, and wilting under stress even with adequate moisture. Damaged roots cannot absorb water and nutrients efficiently.
label: PEST

description: cause curling and yellowing of leaves, secrete honeydew that leads to sooty mold growth, and reduce plant vigor. Heavy infestations can severely stunt plants.   also transmit viral diseases, making them important pests
label: PEST

description: cause silvery stippling (small silvery spots) on leaves due to their rasping-sucking feeding. Leaves become distorted, and fruit size and quality are reduced. Heavy infestations can cause significant economic losses.
label: PEST

description: Look for round, water-soaked, sunken spots on ripening fruit. The spots turn chocolate-colored and depressed. You may see black dots arranged in rings with pinkish-orange powder (spores). These spots appear especially during humid weather.
label: DISEASE

description: appears as small, water-soaked spots on leaves that later turn brown or black. The spots may have a yellow halo around them. On fruits, you'll see raised, dark spots that may ooze bacterial liquid in humid conditions.
label: DISEASE

description: Leaves become curled, twisted, and deformed. You'll notice mosaic patterns (light and dark green patches) on leaves. Plants become stunted and don't grow properly. Fruit yield reduces significantly. This is caused by a virus spread by tiny insects called aphids.
label: DISEASE

description: shows as irregular light and dark green patches on leaves, creating a   pattern. Leaves may also curl and become distorted. Young leaves are more severely affected. The disease is caused by virus and spreads through aphids and infected tools.
label: DISEASE

description: On fruits, you'll see circular rings or spots that are slightly raised. These rings may have different colors from the normal fruit skin. On leaves, circular spots with ring patterns appear. The disease is viral and severely reduces fruit quality and marketability.
label: DISEASE

description: Look for white, cottony or waxy masses on fruits, leaves, and stems. These are clusters of  s. You'll also notice black sooty mold growing on sticky honeydew secreted by bugs. Plants become weak, leaves turn yellow, and growth slows down.
label: PEST

description: Upper leaf surface shows yellow speckling or tiny yellow dots. Lower leaf surface has fine webbing like spider webs. Leaves may turn bronze or brown and dry up. Fruit development reduces. Mites are very tiny and need magnifying glass to see clearly.
label: PEST

description: The base of the stem (crown area) becomes soft, water-soaked, and dark brown or black. Roots rot and plant wilts even with adequate soil moisture. Leaves turn yellow and drop. Young plants may die quickly. The disease spreads in waterlogged soils.
label: DISEASE

description: Fruits develop circular to oval depressed lesions that turn black. The spots may grow and cover the whole fruit. On leaves, you'll see light to dark brown spots with concentric rings (zonate pattern). Crown area may also get infected showing dark lesions.
label: DISEASE

description: attacks fruits, leaves, petioles (leaf stalks), and flowers. On fruits it causes most damage - creating sunken rotten spots. On leaves, brown spots appear. Flowers may rot and drop. The fungus survives on infected plant debris and attacks new growth.
label: DISEASE

description: Treat when: More than 30% of leaves show yellow speckling and webbing; leaves are turning bronze and drying; new growth is affected; fruit setting is reduced. Don't treat if only few leaves have minor yellowing. Monitor weekly by checking lower leaf surface with magnifying glass.
label: PEST

description: First small spots appear, then they become depressed and turn dark brown to black. Spots enlarge in circles and may merge. Severe cases: spots cover entire fruit making it unmarketable. The fungus sporulates on surface creating black powder. Flesh remains firm - unlike anthracnose which causes soft rot.
label: DISEASE

description: Check stem base near soil - if soft, water-soaked, dark brown with foul smell, it's likely  . Plant wilts despite wet soil. Roots are brown and rotten when pulled. Cut stem shows brown discoloration inside. Disease starts at ground level and moves up, unlike other diseases that affect leaves first.
label: DISEASE

description: Two main species: Tetranychus urticae (two-spotted spider mite) and T. cinnabarinus (red spider mite). Both are tiny (0.5 mm), barely visible to naked eye. They live on lower leaf surface, suck plant sap, produce webbing. Look reddish or greenish. Damage symptoms are similar for both species.
label: PEST

description: : lesions remain firm, turn black, don't penetrate deep, fruit flesh stays hard. Anthracnose: lesions become soft, sunken, rot develops, shows pink spore masses, flesh becomes watery. Both need different management - correct identification is important for effective control.
label: DISEASE

description: forms colonies that start at the bottom of the trunk and progress upward into fruits. Heavy infestation causes poor fruit quality and weakens the entire plant. The pest is most damaging on older plants and can cause rejection of export fruits. It's a year-round problem requiring continuous control.
label: PEST

description: Leafhopper causes severe leaf edge yellowing (chlorosis) and browning (necrosis). Leaves become wrinkled, cupped, and may drop. Young plants become stunted. All these symptoms together are called 'hopper burn'. These symptoms look similar to virus disease, so correct identification is important.
label: PEST

description: Three main species: Mediterranean fruit fly (Ceratitis capitata), Oriental fruit fly (Bactrocera dorsalis), and Melon fly (Dacus cucurbitae). All three lay eggs in ripening fruits. Presence of   or their eggs leads to rejection of export shipments to markets like California and Japan.
label: PEST

description: Mealybug injects toxin while feeding, causing leaf yellowing, premature leaf and fruit drop, plant stunting, and deformation. Honeydew buildup attracts ants and causes sooty mold. Seedlings can be killed under heavy infestation. Fruits with mealybugs get rejected at packing plants. Young plants are more susceptible than mature trees.
label: PEST

description: Green peach aphid, melon aphid, and potato aphid transmit the virus when they feed briefly on infected plants then move to healthy plants. Papaya is not a good host for   - they don't colonize it - but even brief feeding spreads virus. You cannot control virus spread by spraying   on papaya trees.
label: PEST

description: parvispinus causes characteristic injury on leaves and fruits. Flowers may drop. Look for silvery streaks on leaves, distorted new growth, and scarring on young fruits.   are very tiny insects - need magnifying glass to see them. They feed by rasping plant tissue and sucking sap.
label: PEST

description: Nematode symptoms include wilting, stunting, decreased plant vigor, reduced yields, and shortened productive life. Root knot   cause swelling and galls on roots. Reniform   reduce root mass. Plants may show symptoms similar to water or nutrient stress. High nematode numbers can exist without visible symptoms.
label: PEST

description: attack newly planted papayas and can destroy entire young plants by feeding on leaves and stems. African snail also climbs mature trees and gets into fruit clusters and growing points. Damage is worst in high rainfall areas with abundant plant litter in the field.
label: PEST

description: Seven main species: Broad mite, papaya leaf edgeroller mite, red and black flat mite, Tuckerellid mites, carmine spider mite, Texas citrus mite, and citrus red mite. Citrus red mite is the main pest in some areas. Broad mites are main pest in cooler areas. Damage includes fruit scarring, leaf drop, and loss of vigor.
label: PEST

description: Both cause similar symptoms - leaf yellowing, cupping, and stunting. Check for presence of tiny leafhoppers (Empoasca stevensi) on leaf undersides. Leafhopper damage usually starts from leaf edges, while virus shows mosaic patterns. Leafhopper symptoms appear during dry weather; virus can occur anytime. Test plants to confirm virus if unsure.
label: PEST

description: Collect soil samples from multiple points in the field before planting. Send to agricultural laboratory for nematode analysis. Lab will identify species and count population levels. This helps you decide if pre-plant fumigation is needed. Test every 2-3 years to monitor nematode buildup.
label: PEST

description: appears as small, water-soaked spots on ripening papaya fruits that enlarge into dark, sunken black lesions. In humid weather, pinkish spore masses may appear on the spots. Infected fruits rot quickly during storage and transport.
label: DISEASE

description: causes small water-soaked lesions on leaves that later turn brown with yellow halos. On fruits, rough scabby spots develop. In severe cases, leaves dry and fall early, reducing fruit yield.
label: DISEASE

description: In leaf curl disease, young leaves become small, curled, thickened, and distorted. The plant becomes stunted and fruiting is poor. This disease is commonly spread by insect vectors like whiteflies and aphids.
label: DISEASE

description: Mosaic disease shows light and dark green mottling on leaves, leaf distortion, reduced leaf size, and stunted plant growth. Fruits may become malformed and yield drops drastically.
label: DISEASE

description: Ringspot disease causes circular ring-like markings on fruits, mosaic patterns on leaves, leaf distortion, and stunted plant growth. Fruits may become deformed and unmarketable.
label: DISEASE

description: Look for three main symptoms: circular patterns on fruit (mottled appearance), yellow mosaic pattern on leaves, and 'shoestring' leaves where leaves become narrow and distorted. The disease is spread by aphids and occurs year-round in Hawaii.
label: DISEASE

description: This is   caused by Colletotrichum gloeosporioides. The fungus infects fruit early but remains hidden (latent) under the fruit skin. Symptoms only become visible when fruits ripen. This is why treating before harvest is important.
label: DISEASE

description: Look for lesions on the trunk with white flecking on the bark. The lesions advance to the core of the central trunk and can kill the tree. Infected fruit develops white spores and rot. This disease is worst during rainy seasons or in areas with poor drainage.
label: DISEASE

description: is present year-round but increases during the wet and cool winter season (mid-October to mid-April) in Hawaii. Spots occur on the lower surface of leaves and on fruit. Red-fleshed varieties are most susceptible. If not controlled, it causes defoliation and reduces fruit sugar and quality.
label: DISEASE

description: is present year-round but worse during periods of moderate temperatures (65-90°F) and humidity. It's mostly a problem on O'ahu and Kaua'i. Red-fleshed varieties like Sunrise are most susceptible. Severely infected leaves dry and fall prematurely, causing loss in plant vigor and reduced fruit quality.
label: DISEASE

description: Pythium is especially challenging during the cool, wet rainy season (mid-October to mid-April) and in locations with high rainfall. It's a significant problem when replanting a field previously planted to papaya. It can destroy seedlings and debilitate fruit-bearing trees under favorable wet or soggy conditions.
label: DISEASE

description: Yellow mosaic pattern on leaves is a symptom of Papaya Ringspot Virus (PRSV). This viral disease also causes mottled fruit with circular patterns and shoestring leaves. The virus is spread by aphids and is present year-round, making it one of the most serious papaya diseases.
label: DISEASE

description: causes small, gray, circular spots mostly on leaves. Under heavy infection, leaves turn yellow and may drop prematurely, affecting fruit quality. Damage to fruit is mostly cosmetic, and fruit rot is not associated with this disease. It's easily controlled when spraying for other diseases.
label: DISEASE

description: This is likely   caused by Rhizopus stolonifer. It's one of the most destructive postharvest diseases because it develops and spreads rapidly. The pathogen enters through wounds during harvest. Symptoms often don't appear until after shipping. High incidence can cause boxes to collapse and shipments to be rejected.
label: DISEASE

description: Several organisms cause   including Alternaria, Stemphylium, Guignardia, and Fusarium. Guignardia is prevalent when fruits are damaged from excessive quarantine heat treatment. Temperatures below 50°F for 15-30 days predispose fruit to most pathogens. Mismanagement of storage temperatures or heat treatment can trigger disease expression.
label: DISEASE

description: is a bacterial disease caused by Enterobacter cloacae. It's an emerging food safety concern because infected fruit affects coliform bacterial counts in papaya cube products. Counts exceeding 100 colony-forming units per gram can result in product rejection, limiting the fresh-cut or frozen products industry.
label: DISEASE

description: or internal blight is caused by Cladosporium, Penicillium, or Fusarium. It results from incomplete closure of the blossom end of the fruit. Premature yellowing can occur if infected. This is a minor disease found on all islands and cannot be treated in the field.
label: DISEASE

description: ing and distortion, especially 'shoestring' leaves, are symptoms of Papaya Ringspot Virus (PRSV). This viral disease also causes yellow mosaic patterns on leaves and mottled fruit. The virus is transmitted by aphids and is the most serious disease problem of papaya.
label: DISEASE

description: While specific mite symptoms aren't detailed in the disease section,   typically causes stippling, bronzing, or silvering of leaves, and may cause leaf drop. Mites are different from fungal diseases and require different control approaches, typically using miticides rather than fungicides.
label: PEST

description: Mealybugs are sap-sucking insects that can weaken plants, cause honeydew secretion leading to sooty mold, and potentially transmit viruses. They appear as white, cottony masses on leaves, stems, and fruit. While not specifically covered in the disease management document, they require insecticide treatment rather than fungicides.
label: PEST

description: (caused by Mycosphaerella, Phoma, Lasiodiplodia, and Phomopsis) occur when spores of fruit-rotting fungi residing on papaya fruit are provided entry points through mechanical injuries or wounds that occur during harvesting, transporting, treating, and packing. The peduncle broken during harvest is a common entry point.
label: DISEASE

description: Yes, both  s and anthracnose are caused by the same fungus, Colletotrichum gloeosporioides. Both are postharvest diseases not apparent at harvest. The fungus becomes established early but remains latent under the fruit cuticle, only becoming visible when fruits ripen. They require the same control measures.
label: DISEASE

description: Mealybugs appear as white cottony clusters on leaf veins, stems, and fruits. Infested plants show yellowing, leaf curling, sticky honeydew on leaves, and black sooty mould growth. Heavy infestation weakens the plant and reduces fruit quality.
label: PEST

description: Mite attack causes fine yellow speckling on leaves, which later turn bronzed and dry. Leaves may curl and drop in severe cases. Fine webbing may be visible on the underside of leaves during heavy infestation.
label: PEST

description: causes yellowing of leaves, wilting, poor growth, and rotting of roots. In severe cases, plants collapse and die, especially in poorly drained, waterlogged soils. Uproot a weak plant and check for brown, decayed roots.
label: DISEASE

description: Infected fruits develop water-soaked patches with white fungal growth. The fruit becomes soft and rots, especially in wet, humid weather. Fallen infected fruits in the field spread the disease further.
label: DISEASE

description: causes dark, circular spots on leaves and fruits. Severe leaf infection leads to leaf fall, which exposes fruits to sunburn and reduces market quality. Disease spreads fast in humid conditions.
label: DISEASE

description: causes brown lesions on leaves and fruits. During wet and humid weather, the disease spreads rapidly, leading to leaf drop, fruit blemishes, downgrading of fruits, and sometimes heavy crop loss.
label: DISEASE

description: appears as dark, sunken spots on ripening fruits. In wet and humid conditions, the spots expand and fruits rot during transport or at market, causing rejection of produce.
label: DISEASE

description: This is likely damping-off disease. Seedlings rot at the base and fall over, especially in warm and wet nursery conditions. Poor hygiene and over-watering increase the problem.
label: DISEASE

description: causes watery, sticky exudate from green fruits. The fruits become unmarketable with poor taste. The disease can spread through pruning tools, harvesting, and infected planting material.
label: DISEASE

description: Mites cause fine yellow specks on leaves, later turning bronze and dry. Leaves may curl and fall. Heavy infestation is common during hot, dry weather.
label: PEST

description: Mealybugs appear as white cottony masses on leaves, stems and fruits. Plants show yellowing, leaf curling and sticky honeydew, which later develops black sooty mould.
label: PEST

description: causes slow growth and older leaves become paler with reduced leaf area and leaf production. Leaf petioles are short, thin and compressed. To correct this, apply foliar spray of urea at 2%. This provides quick nitrogen that plants can absorb through leaves immediately.
label: NUTRIENT

description: causes marked reduction in growth, profusely smaller leaves, leaf margin necrosis and premature yellowing. Purplish brown patches appear at base of petioles. Fruits are badly shaped, poorly filled and unsuitable for marketing. Correct by foliar spray of potassium chloride (KCl) at 2%.
label: NUTRIENT

description: Symptoms show green banding around leaf margin and next to midrib. Leaves turn yellowish-brown at margins. Plant height is reduced, marginal yellowing extends towards midrib. Purplish mottling appears on leaf petioles with leaf malformation. Correct by foliar spray of magnesium sulfate (MgSO4) at 1-2%.
label: NUTRIENT

description: Marginal chlorosis of young leaves appears first, which later turns brown. Fruits develop raised spots that are dark brown or black in color. Leaves give striped appearance from the edges. Correct by foliar spray of manganese sulfate (MnSO4) at 1-2%.
label: NUTRIENT

description: Females lay 150-600 eggs in a white waxy ovisac that is 3-4 times body length. Eggs are greenish yellow and hatch in about 10 days. Nymphs (crawlers) actively search for feeding sites. Adult females are yellow, about 3mm long, covered with white waxy coating. The complete life cycle takes about 3-10 days depending on conditions.
label: PEST

description: Females lay about 300 eggs near veins on underside of leaves. Eggs are small (0.25mm), pear-shaped, white turning brown. Upon hatching, first instar nymphs (crawlers) move to find feeding sites then insert mouthparts to suck plant sap. Adults emerge through T-shaped slit leaving empty pupal cases. Life cycle: eggs 2-8 days, nymphs 9-19 days, pupa 3-30 days, adults 15-30 days.
label: PEST

description: Aphids usually don't lay eggs in warm climates - they reproduce through live birth (viviparity). Nymphs look like wingless adults but smaller and become adults within 7-10 days. Adults are small (1-4mm), soft-bodied with two long antennae. They have cornicles (horns) towards rear of body. Complete generation in 5-10 days at optimal conditions.
label: PEST

description: Female flies insert 10-50 eggs in clusters 1/25 to 1/8 inch below fruit surface. Eggs hatch in 1.5 days. White legless larvae have 3 instars over 11-15 days, feeding on fruit pulp causing rot. Mature larvae drop to soil and pupate for about 10 days. Females begin laying eggs 8 days after emergence and can lay 1,200-3,000 eggs total.
label: PEST

description: Foot rot caused by Phytophthora or Pythium develops in high relative humidity and rainy conditions, especially in sick soil. Resting spores (oospores) germinate and release zoospores which spread with irrigation water throughout the field. Disease is most severe when there is water logging or poor drainage near the stem base.
label: DISEASE

description: Anthracnose spreads through wind-borne conidia and rain splashes. Maximum disease development occurs at about 26°C under wet weather. High relative humidity coupled with higher temperatures favor disease. Infection occurs early in field but remains latent under fruit cuticle, only becoming visible when fruits ripen in storage.
label: DISEASE

description: Powdery mildew develops with relative humidity around 80-85% and temperature range of 24-26°C. The fungus overwinters in dormant buds and produces spores when conditions are favorable in spring. Secondary spread occurs if spores are produced in new infections. White powdery growth appears on undersurface of leaves.
label: DISEASE

description: Papaya ringspot virus is aphid-transmitted - aphids are more active during warmer conditions. It's also mechanically transmitted but not through seeds. Papaya mosaic is mechanically transmissible and aphid-borne. Papaya leaf curl virus is transmitted by whitefly (Bemisia tabaci) and through grafting but not mechanically. Control vectors to prevent virus spread.
label: DISEASE

description: Look for small brown superficial discoloration on fruit skin that develops into circular, slightly sunken areas 1-3 cm in diameter. Under humid conditions, sparse mycelial growth appears on spot margins with salmon pink spores. Remember that infection occurs early but remains hidden under the fruit cuticle, so preventive fungicide sprays are essential before symptoms appear.
label: DISEASE

description: On young fruits, infection causes mummification and deformation. On mature fruits, spots first appear as brown superficial discoloration developing into circular, slightly sunken areas. Lesions gradually coalesce and can cover large areas. Under humid conditions, salmon pink spore masses appear. Lesions develop more slowly on immature fruits than mature ones.
label: DISEASE

description: Black spot appears on the lower surface of leaves and on fruits. Spots occur year-round but are worse during wet, cool winter season (mid-October to mid-April). If not controlled, leaf function is damaged and defoliation occurs, reducing fruit sugar and quality. Red-fleshed varieties are most susceptible. Regular calendar fungicide sprays are required for control.
label: DISEASE

description: Asperisporium black spot is present year-round but increases in intensity during the wet and cool winter season from mid-October to mid-April in Hawaii and similar climates. The combination of high humidity, frequent rain, and moderate temperatures creates ideal conditions for fungal growth and spore production. Increase spray frequency during this period.
label: DISEASE

description: Cercospora black spot causes small, gray, circular spots mostly on leaves. Under heavy infection, leaves turn yellow and drop prematurely. Damage to fruit is mostly cosmetic without fruit rot. Asperisporium causes spots on lower leaf surface and fruits with more severe impact on fruit quality. Both are controlled with similar fungicides when spraying for other diseases.
label: DISEASE

description: Papaya   virus causes curling, crinkling and distortion of leaves, reduction of leaf lamina, rolling of leaf margins inward and downward, and thickening of veins. Leaves become leathery, brittle and distorted. Plants are stunted. Affected plants don't produce flowers and fruits. In advanced stages, defoliation occurs and plant growth is arrested.
label: DISEASE

description: Papaya   virus (PLCV) is in the family Geminiviridae. It cannot be transferred by mechanical means like touching or pruning tools. The virus is readily transmitted through grafting and by whitefly (Bemisia tabaci). Control the whitefly vector to prevent spread. Remove and destroy affected plants immediately as this is the only control measure to reduce disease spread.
label: DISEASE

description: No, affected plants with papaya   virus do not produce flowers and fruits. The virus causes severe stunting and leaf distortion that prevents reproductive development. Sometimes all leaves at the top of the plant show symptoms. In advanced stages, defoliation takes place and growth is completely arrested. This is why immediate removal of infected plants is essential.
label: DISEASE

description: s appear as clusters of cotton-like white waxy masses on leaves, stems, and fruits. Initially affected portions become chlorotic, later turning brown and drying away. Insects excrete honeydew making infested portions shiny and moist. This leads to sooty mold (Capnodium) growth that turns affected parts black, reducing photosynthesis and plant vigor.
label: PEST

description: Papaya   (Paracoccus marginatus) is a polyphagous pest - it attacks many different plant species. Alternate host plants include Hibiscus, bhindi (okra), custard apple, guava and others. This is why removing these alternate hosts from in and around papaya fields throughout the year is an important control measure. The   can move from these plants to papaya.
label: PEST

description: s cause waxy coating on fruits appearing as white cotton-like clusters. They suck plant sap causing chlorosis and reduced plant vigor. Their honeydew secretion leads to black sooty mold covering fruits, making them unmarketable. Severely infested fruits have distorted development. Heavy infestation weakens plants, reduces photosynthesis, and can cause yield loss of 30-50%.
label: PEST

description: Mite damage typically causes stippling (tiny yellow or white spots) on leaves, bronzing or silvering of leaf surfaces, and leaf drop in severe cases. Fine webbing may be visible on leaf undersides. Leaves may curl and become distorted. Mites are tiny (barely visible to naked eye) and suck cell contents, causing leaves to lose green color and appear dusty or dirty.
label: PEST

description: Young seedlings show vein-clearing and downward cupping of leaves about 5 days after infection. A mottle or mosaic pattern develops after 15-20 days. Leaves are reduced in size and show blister-like patches of dark-green tissue alternating with yellowish-green areas. Leaf petioles are shortened and top leaves assume upright position. Plant shows leaf mosaic and stunting.
label: DISEASE

description: Papaya mosaic is caused by mechanically transmissible virus associated with other viral diseases. It is aphid-borne and restricted in host range to papaya and cucurbits. Papaya ringspot virus (PRSV) is more serious, causing shoestring leaves and fruit rings in addition to mosaic. Both are aphid-transmitted, so controlling aphid vectors helps manage both diseases.
label: DISEASE

description: Young seedlings in greenhouse show vein-clearing and downward cupping of leaves about 5 days after inoculation. A mottle or mosaic pattern develops after 15-20 days. Symptoms appear first on young leaves of plants. This timeline helps identify when infection occurred if you can trace back exposure to aphids or mechanical transmission.
label: DISEASE

description: Infected plants initially show chlorosis on youngest leaves followed by vein clearing, rugosity and prominent mottling. Malformation and reduction of leaf lamina occurs which may become extremely filiform (shoestring leaves). Characteristically elongated dark green streaks develop on petioles and upper half of stems. Infected fruits show circular concentric rings. Can cause 56-60% yield loss.
label: DISEASE

description: Infected fruits develop characteristic circular concentric rings on the surface - this is the namesake symptom. Fruits may be malformed, smaller than normal, and have reduced sugar content. Fruit quality is severely affected making them unmarketable. The circular ring patterns are water-soaked lesions that are distinctive and diagnostic for this disease.
label: DISEASE

description: Shoestring leaves are a characteristic symptom of papaya   where leaf lamina (blade) becomes extremely narrow and elongated, resembling a shoestring or ribbon. This occurs due to severe reduction of the leaf lamina. Leaves also show malformation along with vein clearing, chlorosis and mottling. This symptom combined with fruit rings confirms   diagnosis.
label: DISEASE

description: Yes, both chocolate spots and anthracnose are caused by the same fungus Colletotrichum gloeosporioides. They are essentially the same disease with slightly different symptom appearance. Both occur as postharvest diseases not apparent at harvest time. The fungus becomes established earlier but remains latent under fruit cuticle, only becoming visible when fruits ripen.
label: DISEASE

description: Virus diseases show mosaic patterns, vein clearing, leaf distortion, shoestring leaves, and stunting affecting whole plants with irregular field distribution. Nutrient deficiencies show uniform yellowing or specific patterns (interveinal chlorosis), affect all plants in area uniformly, and respond quickly to fertilizer application. Virus symptoms don't improve with nutrition. Test soil and observe field patterns to distinguish.
label: DISEASE

description: Yes, mixed infections with multiple viruses can occur in papaya. When both ringspot (PRSV) and mosaic viruses infect the same plant, symptoms may be more severe with combined characteristics - severe leaf distortion, pronounced mottling, stunting, and poor fruit quality. Both are aphid-transmitted, so controlling aphid vectors and removing infected plants promptly helps prevent both diseases.
label: DISEASE

description: Early stage: initial curling and crinkling starts on younger leaves with slight reduction of leaf lamina. Middle stage: rolling of leaf margins inward and downward, thickening of veins, leaves become leathery and brittle. Late stage: severe distortion, all top leaves affected, defoliation begins, growth arrested, no flowering or fruiting. Sometimes all leaves at top show symptoms simultaneously. Plant eventually dies if not removed.
label: DISEASE

description: Eggs: Greenish yellow, found in white waxy ovisac that is 3-4 times body length (150-600 eggs). Nymphs (crawlers): Small, mobile, searching for feeding sites, hatch in 10 days. Adult females: Yellow, 3mm long, 1.4mm wide, covered with white waxy coating, stationary. Adult males: Pink (especially pre-pupal and pupal stages), about 1.0mm long, winged. Complete life cycle 3-10 days.
label: PEST

description: Characteristically elongated dark green streaks develop on petioles and upper half of the stems. These streaks are water-soaked in appearance and are diagnostic for   along with leaf and fruit symptoms. The streaks run longitudinally (lengthwise) along the stem and are most prominent on younger, upper portions of the plant where active growth is occurring.
label: DISEASE

description: Whiteflies are tiny white insects found on the underside of leaves. They suck plant sap, causing yellowing and curling of leaves. Sticky honeydew is deposited, leading to black sooty mould on leaves.
label: PEST

description: lays eggs in semi-ripe fruits. Maggots feed inside, causing soft rotting patches, oozing of fluid, and premature fruit drop. A small puncture mark may be visible on fruit surface.
label: PEST

description: Aphids are small green or black insects found in clusters on tender leaves and shoots. They suck sap, causing leaf curling, yellowing, stunted growth, and honeydew deposition leading to sooty mould.
label: PEST

description: Mite infestation becomes severe during hot and dry weather. Dusty conditions favour rapid multiplication of mites, leading to bronzing and drying of leaves.
label: PEST

description: grubs feed on roots causing wilting of young plants, while adults notch leaf margins. Severe infestation can lead to poor plant establishment.
label: PEST

description: Mosaic disease shows irregular light and dark green patches with leaf distortion and stunted growth, while nutrient deficiency usually shows uniform yellowing without leaf distortion. Mosaic patterns are patchy and uneven.
label: DISEASE

description: Ringspot shows circular ring-like markings on fruit surface. Leaves show mosaic and distortion. Fruits become deformed and unmarketable in severe infection.
label: DISEASE

description: lesions often have water-soaked margins and yellow halos, while fungal spots are usually dry with concentric rings.  s spread rapidly after rain or overhead irrigation.
label: DISEASE

description: Look for small white cottony clusters on leaf veins and tender shoots. Early detection helps control before heavy honeydew and sooty mould develop.
label: PEST

description: Early signs include tiny yellow speckles on leaves, slight bronzing, and rough leaf texture. Check the underside of leaves for fine webbing.
label: PEST

description: Young leaves start curling upward, become smaller and thicker, and the plant growth slows down. Early detection helps in removing infected plants before virus spreads.
label: DISEASE

description: Early symptoms include light and dark green mottling on young leaves, slight leaf distortion, and uneven leaf color. Symptoms worsen with plant age.
label: DISEASE

description: Early symptoms include mosaic patterns on leaves, mild leaf distortion, and faint ring-like markings starting to appear on young fruits.
label: DISEASE

description: on peach shows pale-green spots turning light brown with a yellowish halo. Spots may merge, darken, dry out, and create a shot-hole effect.
label: DISEASE

description: Typical symptoms of   on peach leaves: pale-green spots turning light brown with a yellowish halo. Spots may merge, darken, dry out, and create a shot-hole effect.
label: DISEASE

description: is one of the peach leaf problems the photo check recognises. The training data has no symptom description for it; ask a local agriculture officer to confirm.
label: DISEASE

description: is one of the pear leaf problems the photo check recognises. The training data has no symptom description for it; ask a local agriculture officer to confirm.
label: DISEASE

description: Alternaria appears as small dark brown to black spots on leaves that gradually enlarge with yellow halos. In severe cases, spots merge causing leaf drying and premature leaf fall. Fruits may show dark sunken lesions.
label: DISEASE

description: causes small water-soaked spots on fruits that turn dark brown to black and become sunken. In humid conditions, pinkish spore masses may appear on lesions. Infected fruits crack and rot.
label: DISEASE

description: causes water-soaked angular spots on leaves that turn dark brown with yellow halos. On fruits, black raised lesions appear and cracks develop, reducing market value.
label: DISEASE

description: Cercospora causes small circular to irregular greyish-brown spots on leaves with dark margins. In severe infection, leaves turn yellow and drop early.
label: DISEASE

description: Look for small water-soaked, dark colored irregular spots on leaves. These spots can appear as one or several on each leaf. In severe cases, you'll notice premature leaf drop. The spots have an oily appearance and are slightly raised. On fruits, they appear as dark brown irregular spots that may split open with L-shaped cracks.
label: DISEASE

description: appears as small, regular to irregular black spots on leaves, calyx region, and fruits. These spots later turn dark brown and become depressed (sunken). On fruits, you'll see dark brown depressed spots that make the fruit look damaged. Infected leaves turn yellow and eventually drop off. The disease is most visible during August-September.
label: DISEASE

description: starts as minute, brown spots with a yellow halo around them. The spots are scattered across the leaf, appearing circular or irregular in shape. As they age, they become dark brown. On the lower surface of leaves, spots appear sunken with greyish clusters of spore-bearing structures. On flowers, you'll see minute, circular, black spots on the sepals. Fruit spots are black, minute, circular, and later become large, irregularly circular, and depressed, giving fruits an ugly appearance.
label: DISEASE

description: While the document focuses on other diseases, Alternaria typically appears as dark brown to black spots with concentric rings (target-like pattern) on leaves. The spots may have a yellow halo and can cause premature leaf drop. On fruits, it causes dark, sunken lesions. If you see these symptoms along with the diseases mentioned in your IPM guide, consult with local agricultural extension officers for confirmation.
label: DISEASE

description: Yes, this could be  . The main symptoms are: 1) Yellowing of leaves on some twigs or branches, 2) Drooping and drying of leaves following the yellowing, 3) The entire tree may die within a few months to a year. To confirm, cut open the affected tree lengthwise or in cross-section - you'll see dark grayish-brown discoloration of the wood inside. This vascular discoloration is a definitive sign of  .
label: DISEASE

description: Look for these signs: 1) Small holes bored into young fruits (usually visible as entry points), 2) The caterpillar feeds inside on pulp and seeds, leaving the fruit hollow, 3) Affected fruits start rotting from inside, 4) Premature fruit drop is common, 5) You might see dark brown, short, hairy caterpillars if you cut open damaged fruits. The adult is a bluish-brown butterfly. This pest is most prevalent during the 'mrig' bahar season (June to February), with fruit injury visible when fruits are 30-50 days old.
label: PEST

description: Both nymphs and adults feed on the underside of leaves by rasping the surface and sucking cell sap. The damage appears as: 1) Leaf tips turning brown and curling, 2) Drying and shedding of flowers - this directly reduces fruit set, 3) Scab formation on fruits which significantly reduces market value and quality. The insects are minute (1.4 mm), slender, and soft-bodied with fringed wings. They appear straw yellow to blackish brown. Incidence is mainly from July to October with peak in September.
label: PEST

description: Female  s lay 109-185 eggs in groups beneath their body in a loose waxy covering (ovisac). The oviposition period is 20-29 days. Eggs hatch in just 3-4 hours. Female nymphs molt 3 times over 26-47 days, while male nymphs molt 4 times over 31-57 days to become adults. Adult females live 36-53 days, but males live only 1-3 days. Moist and warm conditions favor rapid multiplication. The entire population can build up quickly under favorable conditions.
label: PEST

description: are small yellowish-green insects that suck sap from leaves, shoots, and fruits. Damage includes: 1) Yellowing of leaves due to sap loss, 2) Wilting of terminal shoots, 3) Stunted growth, 4) Honeydew secretion leading to sooty mold growth on leaves and fruits, 5) Curling and distortion of young leaves. They typically colonize the upper sides of mature leaves, concentrated along midribs and leaf margins, and are also found on flowers but rarely on fruits.
label: PEST

description: Whiteflies are small, powdery white insects active during early morning. Both nymphs and adults suck sap from leaves, causing: 1) Yellowing and dropping of affected leaves, 2) Honeydew secretion on leaf surfaces, 3) Development of sooty mold fungus on honeydew, giving leaves a black appearance, 4) Reduced photosynthesis and plant vigor, 5) Weakened plants more susceptible to diseases. The nymphs have short glass-like rods of wax along their body sides.
label: PEST

description: Look for these signs: 1) Small shot-like holes (2-3 mm diameter) on the bark of main trunk, roots, and lower branches, 2) Fine powdery boring dust near holes, 3) Wilting of branches above the borer entry points, 4) Progressive death of tree if infestation is severe, 5) Multiple holes appearing like gunshot wounds on bark. Adult beetles are 2-3 mm long, black to reddish-brown, and cigar-shaped. Infested young plants should be uprooted and burnt immediately.
label: PEST

description: The female lays 20-40 eggs in young living plants, deposited under the bark of stems. Newly emerged larvae are about 6 mm (1/4 inch) long, growing to about 63 mm (2.5 inches) when mature. The larva feeds on soft tissues around the egg cavity then bores into stem and roots, developing for 9-10 months. The pupal period is 16-18 days. Adults are pale yellowish-brown beetles 30-35 mm long with light grey elytra having numerous black spots. They emerge by eating a circular hole through the bark. There is only one generation per year, and adult beetles live 45-60 days.
label: PEST

description: Watch for these symptoms: 1) Holes on the bark of main stems with excreta visible, 2) Dry powdered material (frass) near the base of plants, 3) Galleries visible if bark is peeled, 4) Progressive drying and wilting of branches, 5) Weakened structural integrity of stems and branches, 6) Adult beetles gnawing the green bark of shoots during the day. description: Boron is the most commonly deficient micronutrient in strawberry plantings because it is very prone to leaching. description: shows early symptoms similar to leaf spot, but the spots become angular or irregular and the centers remain dark purple instead of turning white. The entire leaf may become reddish or light purple. Look for these purple-centered angular spots on leaves, particularly during warm weather. The disease can also affect fruits, petioles, runners, fruit stalks and berry calyxes.
