description: fruit rot (black spot) first appears as white, water-soaked lesions up to 3 mm in diameter on all stages of fruit. These lesions become brown and eventually encompass the whole fruit. The lesions contain distinctive salmon-colored spore masses. Infected fruit eventually dry to hard, black, shriveled mummies. The disease is caused by Colletotrichum species and can attack foliage, runners, crowns and fruit.
label: DISEASE

description: On stems and runners,   causes girdling lesions that contain salmon-colored masses of spores. Infected crowns turn reddish-brown, and the entire plant may wilt and die. This is particularly serious as crown infection can kill the whole plant, making early detection critical for plant survival.
label: DISEASE

description: (Botrytis fruit rot) is the most serious fruit rot in strawberries. Infected young blossoms show browning and drying (blasting) that travels down the pedicel. On fruit, infections appear as soft, light brown, rapidly enlarging areas. Fruit eventually become covered with a grey, dusty powder - hence the name. The fungus initially colonizes dying flowers during bloom, enters green fruit through flowers and remains inactive until fruit matures. Spread is rapid through handling, and healthy berries can become a rotted mass within 48 hours.
label: DISEASE

description: , caused by Mycosphaerella fragariae, is probably the most widespread leaf disease of strawberries. Look for dark purple to reddish-purple spots (5-10 mm wide) on upper leaf surfaces. The centers of these spots turn tan or grey and eventually white - this white center distinguishes it from leaf scorch. Late in the season, tan or bluish areas form on leaf undersurfaces. In warm weather, one or two black spots (black seed disease) may form on fruit. The organism can infect leaves, fruits, petioles, runners, fruit stalks and berry calyxes.
label: DISEASE

description: , caused by Phomopsis obscurans, is most common after harvest. It's distinct from leaf spot and leaf scorch - the infected area becomes V-shaped with the widest part at the leaf margin. Spots are initially reddish-purple and develop a darker brown or reddish-brown center surrounded by light brown area with purple border. Leaves can eventually become blighted and die. The fungus also infects fruit caps with similar symptoms and can cause a soft, pale pink rot at fruit ends.
label: DISEASE

description: First symptoms are curling of leaf edges, followed by dry purplish to brownish patches on leaf undersurfaces. As disease progresses, patches of white, powdery fungus mycelium develop on undersides of leaves and reddish discoloration appears on upper surfaces. Infected fruit become hard and fail to ripen normally. The disease is facilitated by temperatures of 15-27°C and moderate to high humidity.
label: DISEASE

description: , caused by Phytophthora cactorum, can infect fruit at any development stage. In green fruit, diseased areas are dark brown or natural green outlined with brown margin, and the whole berry eventually becomes brown with rough texture and leathery appearance. Infected ripe fruit show less dramatic symptoms but can be identified by duller color, bitter taste and marked darkening of xylem connections to seeds. Eventually mature fruits become tough and leathery, sometimes with white moldy growth. The disease is usually serious only during excessive rain in temperate regions.
label: DISEASE

description: Red stele (red core), caused by Phytophthora fragariae, causes stunted plants that produce few runners and lose normal shiny green luster. Younger leaves have metallic bluish-green color, while older leaves turn yellow or red. During hot, dry periods, diseased plants rapidly wilt and die. They produce few roots and the stele (core) of roots is pink to brick red - this is the diagnostic symptom. The disease is particularly troublesome in heavy clay soils saturated with water during cool seasons, with optimal development at 13-15°C.
label: DISEASE

description: causes leaves to wilt rapidly, dry and become reddish-yellow or dark brown. Few leaves and runners are formed. New roots are dwarfed with blackened tips. In new plantings, symptoms begin to appear as runners form, whereas in established plantings symptoms are most prevalent just before picking. The disease is caused by Verticillium albo-atrum and V. dahliae, which can remain alive in field for up to 25 years.
label: DISEASE

description: is caused by a complex of organisms including Pythium and Rhizoctonia species. Affected roots show: 1) Much smaller root systems than normal. 2) Main roots spotted with dark patches or zones. 3) Most feeder roots lacking. 4) All or part of main root dead and blackened throughout. Plants are less vigorous and produce few runners. Often associated with nematodes, winter injury, fertilizer burn, soil compaction, herbicide damage, drought, excess salt, waterlogging or improper soil pH. Can affect scattered plants or localized regions within fields.
label: DISEASE

description: , caused by Macrophomina phaseolina, has become widespread problem in California and Florida since methyl bromide fumigation was phased out. Symptoms usually appear after plants are well established and have started producing fruit. Older leaves begin to wilt and turn grey-green, then dry up. As disease progresses, all foliage eventually collapses and dries up except central, youngest leaves. Vascular and cortical tissues of crowns turn dark brown to orange-brown, along with main roots. Severe outbreaks reported in Argentina, Italy, Spain, Turkey, Greece and Israel.
label: DISEASE

description: , caused by Fusarium oxysporum f. sp. fragariae, emerged as problem in California after methyl bromide fumigation stopped. Symptoms can appear as early as 30 days after transplanting when plants stop growing and appear stunted. As disease progresses, virtually all foliage collapses and dries except central, youngest leaves. Vascular and cortical tissues turn dark brown to orange-brown, similar to charcoal wilt. There are no field symptoms to separate Fusarium from charcoal wilt - affected plants must be tested by plant pathology laboratory for definitive diagnosis.
label: DISEASE

description: (vascular collapse) is caused by a distinct pathotype of Phytophthora cactorum - the same organism that causes leather rot on fruit. Young leaves wilt suddenly, turn brown and whole plant dies within a few days. Crowns break easily at their tops, leaving most of crown behind. Crowns are brown with disintegrated vascular tissue. Infection occurs primarily in runnering bed or after transplanting. Most susceptible when temperatures are high in early to mid-summer, soil drainage is poor and plants are stressed. Cultivars vary greatly in susceptibility.
label: DISEASE

description: Main virus groups: 1) Aphid-transmitted: Strawberry mild yellow-edge (SMYEV), vein banding (SVBV), crinkle (SCV), mottle (SMoV), and others. SCV causes chlorotic spotting and crinkled leaves. SMoV causes small chlorotic spots and mild mottling. SMYEV shows marginal chlorosis and leaf cupping. 2) Whitefly-transmitted criniviruses. 3) Pollen-borne ilarviruses including strawberry necrotic shock virus. 4) Nematode-transmitted nepoviruses like tomato ringspot and strawberry latent ringspot viruses. Multiple virus infections act synergistically causing severe reductions in vigor, runner production and yield.
label: DISEASE

description: transmitted by leaf hoppers: 1) Aster yellows - older leaves turn red, lie flat on ground, plant usually dead within 2 months. Common in North America, Europe, Australasia, Japan and Russia. 2) Green petal disease (clover phyllody) - most obvious symptom is production of virescent and adherent green petals that later turn red, and fruits become 'buttoned'. Found in north-eastern North America, Europe and Australia. Both caused by phytoplasma in aster yellows taxonomic groups.
label: DISEASE

description: (Paria fragariae) is widespread pest. In some locations, most damaging as adult leaf feeder; in others, most severely damages roots as larvae. They overwinter in mulch and soil crevices, become active in May and June. Adults chew small holes in leaves at night ('shot holes'). Females lay eggs in leaves near soil surface. Larvae burrow through soil to roots where they feed until mid-summer when they emerge and feed on leaves. Heavy infestations result in leaves riddled with small holes. Both larval root feeding and adult leaf feeding reduce plant vigor.
label: PEST

description: , caused by Alternaria alternata f. fragariae, occurs in Europe, New Zealand, Korea and Japan. It causes localized economic problems in these regions. Lesions appear on upper leaves as circular or irregular patches (2-5 mm) that are brown with dark purplish margins. This disease is distinct from the common leaf spot and leaf scorch found in North America. Controlled through same general cultural practices as other leaf diseases - sanitation, air circulation, and resistant varieties where available.
label: DISEASE

description: (hard rot), caused by Rhizoctonia solani, is important pathogen of many worldwide crops. In strawberries, it's most severe where fruit are allowed to touch soil. Symptoms include light brown fruit that soften and collapse, with their juices leaking out. The same organism also causes Rhizoctonia root rot where plants suddenly collapse during early fruiting. Undersides of leaves become purplish and numerous side crowns formed around dead ones. Control by using mulch to prevent fruit-soil contact and maintaining good drainage.
label: DISEASE

description: (leak), caused by Rhizopus species, can occur worldwide and has caused severe problems in UK preserve industry. Symptoms include slightly discolored fruits that gradually turn light brown. Fruit eventually collapse, become covered with dense, fluffy mycelium and their juices leak out - hence name 'leak'. The importance of   is GREATLY DIMINISHED BY RAPID COOLING AFTER HARVEST. This is key control measure. Proper post-harvest handling - immediate cooling and refrigeration - is more important than field control for this disease.
label: DISEASE

description: , caused by Sclerotina sclerotiorum, is primarily crown rotting organism in southern USA but can also affect fruit (Sclerotina rot). Both crowns and fruit become covered with dense white mycelium containing sclerotia - hard, black survival structures. This distinguishes it from grey mould which has grey, dusty spores rather than sclerotia. The sclerotia can survive in soil for years, making crop rotation important. Most problematic in areas with mild winters where sclerotia survive well.
label: DISEASE

description: Phomopsis (Dendrophoma) soft rot, caused by Phomopsis obscurans, is very important fruit rot in Florida. The same organism also causes leaf blight. On fruit, it's commonly associated with stem-end rot and appears initially as light pink, water-soaked lesions that eventually turn brown with crusty centers. This pink appearance distinguishes it from other fruit rots. Can be serious in warm, humid conditions. Control through fungicides, sanitation, and avoiding conditions that favor the disease.
